Keep consumers current: Configure an appropriate rotation workflow and consumer refresh strategy. Existing environment variables, connections and application caches may retain older values until refreshed or restarted.
03.decisionCue: A dynamic reference avoids plaintext templates; rotation and consumer refresh still need design.

03.title: Cross-account secret reads must pass three authorization gates
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Caller identity permission: The consuming account's principal needs appropriate secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission for the intended secret ARN and context. Secret resource policy: The secret owner must grant the intended external principal access through a supported resource-based policy. Scope principals and conditions; avoid unintended external sharing. Customer-managed KMS key: For a secret encrypted with the owner's customer-managed key, permit the consumer's required decrypt use in applicable key/IAM policies. A secret permission alone does not authorize its encryption key.
learningNotes: Caller identity permission: The consuming account's principal needs appropriate secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission for the intended secret ARN and context.

Secret resource policy: The secret owner must grant the intended external principal access through a supported resource-based policy. Scope principals and conditions; avoid unintended external sharing.

Customer-managed KMS key: For a secret encrypted with the owner's customer-managed key, permit the consumer's required decrypt use in applicable key/IAM policies. A secret permission alone does not authorize its encryption key.
03.decisionCue: Cross-account access needs permission to the secret and permission to use its key.

03.title: KMS key material origin is different from key ownership
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. AWS-generated or imported: A customer-managed key can use AWS-generated material or supported imported material. Imported-material expiry, deletion and reimport behavior require an explicit availability and recovery plan. CloudHSM custom key store: A supported custom key store backs KMS operations with a connected CloudHSM cluster. KMS integration remains, while cluster availability, capacity and operations become dependencies. External key store: An external key store delegates supported cryptographic operations to an external key manager through its proxy. This is different from importing material into KMS; latency and external outages affect AWS workloads.
learningNotes: AWS-generated or imported: A customer-managed key can use AWS-generated material or supported imported material. Imported-material expiry, deletion and reimport behavior require an explicit availability and recovery plan.

CloudHSM custom key store: A supported custom key store backs KMS operations with a connected CloudHSM cluster. KMS integration remains, while cluster availability, capacity and operations become dependencies.

External key store: An external key store delegates supported cryptographic operations to an external key manager through its proxy. This is different from importing material into KMS; latency and external outages affect AWS workloads.
03.decisionCue: Ownership, material origin and the location performing cryptographic operations are separate decisions.

03.title: CloudHSM TLS offload: keep the private key in the HSM
03.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Locate TLS termination: An ALB can terminate supported TLS with its configured certificate. A server-side TLS design instead terminates the connection at the application server; these are different key-placement choices. Use a supported HSM integration: For a supported web-server/cryptographic integration, an EC2 application invokes CloudHSM-backed private-key operations through the client/provider stack. CloudHSM does not become a transparent network proxy in the traffic path. Operate the dependency: Plan the HSM cluster, client configuration, private connectivity, certificate deployment and application recovery. HSM-backed keys do not remove TLS policy, trust-chain or availability responsibilities.

Use a supported HSM integration: For a supported web-server/cryptographic integration, an EC2 application invokes CloudHSM-backed private-key operations through the client/provider stack. CloudHSM does not become a transparent network proxy in the traffic path.

Operate the dependency: Plan the HSM cluster, client configuration, private connectivity, certificate deployment and application recovery. HSM-backed keys do not remove TLS policy, trust-chain or availability responsibilities.
03.decisionCue: Identify where the TLS session terminates and which system can use its private key.

04.title: VPC boundary, CIDR and route-table mental model
04.imageBrief: VPC boundary, CIDR and route-table mental model — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: A VPC CIDR contains subnets in one Availability Zone each. Route tables choose a next hop for destination prefixes.
A route and matching security permissions are both needed for a viable traffic path.
04.decisionCue: Trace the address range, route, then security boundary.

04.title: Public and private subnet paths
04.imageBrief: Public and private subnet paths — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Public, private and isolated subnet roles follow their effective routes. Direct IPv4 internet access also needs a public IPv4 address.
Private IPv4 outbound uses a NAT Gateway in a public subnet; an isolated database has no internet route.
04.decisionCue: Read the route table before classifying a subnet.

04.title: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway and egress-only IGW
04.imageBrief: Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway and egress-only IGW — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: An IGW route and public IPv4 address enable direct public IPv4 access, subject to security controls.
NAT Gateway translates private IPv4 outbound; egress-only IGW allows initiated IPv6 outbound without translation.
04.decisionCue: Choose the exit by address family and inbound requirement.

04.title: Subnet sizing and address growth
04.imageBrief: Subnet sizing and address growth — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: AWS reserves five IPv4 addresses per subnet: first four and last. /24 yields 251 usable; /22 yields 1019.
Subnet CIDR size cannot change after creation; leave nonoverlapping space for AZ growth and ENIs.
04.decisionCue: Plan CIDRs for later growth, not only current hosts.

04.title: IPAM pools and allocation governance
04.imageBrief: IPAM pools and allocation governance — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: IPAM organizes address space into scopes and pools with governed allocation across accounts and Regions.
Monitor utilization and overlap; IPAM does not automatically renumber existing networks.
04.decisionCue: Centralize allocation before multi-account VPC growth.

04.title: Overlap detection and network renumbering
04.imageBrief: Overlap detection and network renumbering — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Overlapping VPC CIDRs prevent unambiguous direct routing and VPC peering.
IPAM reveals conflicts; plan workload and DNS migration to nonoverlapping space. PrivateLink can expose a specific service without full network connectivity.
04.decisionCue: Identify overlap before interconnecting networks.

04.title: Route priority and longest-prefix match
04.imageBrief: Route priority and longest-prefix match — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Longest-prefix match selects the most specific route in the associated subnet route table.
Check return routes and SG/NACL permissions after selecting a target.
04.decisionCue: Read the effective route table for the source subnet.

04.title: Security groups versus network ACLs
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the enforcement boundary: Security groups attach to supported resources/ENIs and are stateful. Network ACLs apply at the subnet boundary and are stateless. A route and both applicable control layers must permit the intended path. Evaluate the rule model: Security groups use allow rules with implicit denial otherwise. Network ACLs support numbered allow/deny rules, evaluated in ascending order until a match; the first matching rule determines the result. Validate the return flow: Stateful security-group tracking normally permits response traffic for an allowed connection. NACLs need explicit return-direction rules, including the actual client ephemeral-port range; do not assume one OS's range fits every client.

04.decisionCue: Statefulness changes return-traffic behavior; it does not create a route.

04.title: VPC Flow Logs: what they show and miss
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the observation scope: Create supported flow logging at VPC, subnet or ENI scope. Records summarize observed network flows and can be delivered to supported destinations such as CloudWatch Logs or S3. Read network evidence: Inspect interface, addresses, ports, protocol, byte/packet counts, time range, action and log status. Correlate forward and return directions; ACCEPT/REJECT alone does not identify every security or routing cause. Know the blind spots: Flow Logs are not packet captures, payload inspection or proof of application success. Some traffic is excluded, records may be delayed or skipped, and no flow record can also mean the packet never reached that observation point.

04.decisionCue: A flow record is evidence at an interface, not a complete end-to-end diagnosis.

04.title: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface
04.imageBrief: VPC endpoints: gateway versus interface — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Gateway endpoints use route table targets for S3 and DynamoDB and have no endpoint hourly charge.
Interface endpoints create managed ENIs with security groups and can support private DNS and hybrid access with routing/DNS.
04.decisionCue: Pick endpoint type by service, reachability and cost.

04.title: Private DNS for interface endpoints
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Resolve to the private interface: With supported private DNS enabled, the normal service hostname resolves to the endpoint's private addresses within the configured DNS scope. This changes name resolution, not the application's IAM permissions. Prepare VPC and hybrid DNS: Check VPC DNS settings, private-zone conflicts and supported Resolver forwarding for other VPCs or on-premises clients. Creating an endpoint in one VPC does not automatically redirect every external client's DNS. Prove the complete request: Verify the resolved address, route, endpoint security group and applicable endpoint/resource/identity policies. Private addressing alone does not prove the intended access path or authorization.

04.decisionCue: Private DNS selects an address; networking and authorization still have to work.

04.title: Endpoint policies and resource policies
04.imageBrief: Endpoint policies and resource policies — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: IAM identity permissions, endpoint policy, bucket/resource policy and applicable SCPs jointly determine access; explicit Deny prevails.
An endpoint policy filters but does not grant permissions alone; same-account identity permission need not require separate bucket-policy Allow.
04.decisionCue: Trace principal, action, resource and path.

04.title: VPC peering and nontransitive routes
04.imageBrief: VPC peering and nontransitive routes — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Peering connects two nonoverlapping VPCs directly, including across accounts/Regions.
It is nontransitive: A↔B and B↔C do not enable A↔C. Routes and security permissions are needed in both VPCs.
04.decisionCue: Use direct peerings sparingly; consider TGW for transit.

04.title: Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke attachments
04.imageBrief: Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke attachments — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A regional Transit Gateway attaches VPCs and hybrid networks. A subnet route sends traffic to TGW; its associated TGW route table selects an attachment.
Reachability depends on association, propagation/static routes, destination return route and security controls.
04.decisionCue: Trace both directions through VPC and TGW routes.

04.title: Transit Gateway route tables and segmentation
04.imageBrief: Transit Gateway route tables and segmentation — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Each attachment consults its associated TGW route table for incoming traffic. Propagation or static routes populate selected destination paths.
Separate tables can allow Prod and Dev to reach shared services without allowing direct Prod↔Dev routing.
04.decisionCue: Validate forward and return paths for each segment.

04.title: Cross-account Transit Gateway sharing
04.imageBrief: Cross-account Transit Gateway sharing — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A network account can share a regional TGW through AWS RAM with workload accounts, which create VPC attachments.
TGW owner controls route tables, associations and propagation; VPC routes and security controls remain separate.
04.decisionCue: Share the hub, then deliberately attach and route.

04.title: Cloud WAN core network and policy
04.imageBrief: Cloud WAN core network and policy — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Cloud WAN uses a global core network policy with regional edges, segments and attachment mapping.
Segment isolation and route sharing are policy decisions; do not assume automatic reachability.
04.decisionCue: Compare global policy needs with regional TGW hubs.

04.title: PrivateLink producer and consumer boundaries
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink producer and consumer boundaries — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: PrivateLink exposes a particular provider service through an interface endpoint without full VPC peering or CIDR routing.
Overlapping provider and consumer VPC CIDRs can work for service-level access.
04.decisionCue: Use for a specific private service across account boundaries.

04.title: PrivateLink endpoint service and NLB
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink endpoint service and NLB — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Provider associates an NLB with an endpoint service and manages allowed principals/acceptance.
Consumer creates interface endpoints in supported AZs and checks endpoint SG, DNS and service health.
04.decisionCue: Test both provider target health and consumer endpoint state.

04.title: PrivateLink versus peering versus Transit Gateway
04.imageBrief: PrivateLink versus peering versus Transit Gateway — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Peering provides direct nontransitive VPC routing; TGW centralizes many routed VPC/hybrid links; PrivateLink publishes a service only.
Choose according to needed reachability, overlap, security and cost.
04.decisionCue: Ask whether the consumer needs a network, routed hub or service.

04.title: VPC Lattice service-network connectivity
04.imageBrief: VPC Lattice service-network connectivity — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Lattice associates client VPCs and application services with a service network.
Listeners, target groups, optional IAM authorization and observability organize access across accounts.
04.decisionCue: Choose service networking for managed application access.

04.title: Lattice authentication, routing and observability
04.imageBrief: Lattice authentication, routing and observability — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: AWS_IAM auth uses signed requests and applicable service/service-network policies; NONE leaves Lattice authorization unenforced.
Rules and default actions select forwarding; inspect target health, access logs and metrics.
04.decisionCue: Trace authorization, routing and target health separately.

04.title: Centralized ingress and shared services VPC
04.imageBrief: Centralized ingress and shared services VPC — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: A central ingress ALB can use supported reachable private IP targets across connected VPCs.
Shared services and application VPCs need explicit routes, return paths and security controls; evaluate central failure domains.
04.decisionCue: Prove IP target health and return routing.

04.title: Centralized egress and NAT design
04.imageBrief: Centralized egress and NAT design — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.2.
learningNotes: Spokes route through TGW to an egress VPC with public NAT Gateway and IGW.
Return routes, AZ alignment and TGW/NAT/cross-AZ cost need explicit design; NAT does not perform deep inspection.
04.decisionCue: Compare resilience and total traffic cost before centralizing.

04.title: Inspection VPC and symmetric routing
04.imageBrief: Inspection VPC and symmetric routing — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Stateful inspection requires forward and return traffic through the same flow-state endpoint.
Inspection VPC TGW appliance mode supports symmetry; native TGW-attached Network Firewall provides another managed option.
04.decisionCue: Validate route symmetry before changing firewall rules.

04.title: Gateway Load Balancer appliance insertion
04.imageBrief: Gateway Load Balancer appliance insertion — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: GWLB distributes flows to healthy third-party appliances with GENEVE encapsulation on UDP 6081.
GWLBe is the route target; inspection round trip returns through GWLB/GWLBe before VPC forwarding. Validate flow symmetry.
04.decisionCue: Separate steering from the appliance's inspection function.

04.title: AWS Network Firewall rule and endpoint path
04.imageBrief: AWS Network Firewall rule and endpoint path — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Network Firewall policy links stateless and stateful rule groups; stateless forward-to-stateful and stateful ordering/defaults affect evaluation.
Choose routed VPC endpoints/inspection VPC or native TGW network function attachment; the latter uses static routing and managed symmetry.
04.decisionCue: Validate placement, rule evaluation and flow/alert logs.

04.title: AWS WAF at application ingress
04.imageBrief: AWS WAF at application ingress — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: WAF inspects supported HTTP(S) requests using web ACL managed/custom/rate-based rules.
Allow/Block terminate, Count continues, and default action applies when no terminating action occurs. Tune with logs before enforcement.
04.decisionCue: Choose layer 7 protection and test false positives.

04.title: DDoS protection and edge placement
04.imageBrief: DDoS protection and edge placement — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Shield Standard provides baseline DDoS protection; Advanced adds capabilities for eligible protected resources under subscription.
Combine suitable edge services, origin restrictions, WAF, resilient applications, alarms and incident response.
04.decisionCue: Reduce origin exposure and validate operational readiness.

04.title: Layered segmentation and data perimeter
04.imageBrief: Layered segmentation and data perimeter — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Routing and SG/NACL/firewall controls apply to network boundaries; IAM/resource/endpoint policies authorize identities, resources and paths.
For S3, a bucket policy can require an approved endpoint. Test service-to-service access and supported condition keys.
04.decisionCue: Authorize identity, resource and trusted path.

04.title: IPv6 addressing and subnet allocation
04.imageBrief: IPv6 addressing and subnet allocation — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Plan IPv6 allocation independently of IPv4; /56 to subnet /64 is an example, not a universal allocation requirement.
IPv6 needs addresses, supported services, routes and IPv6 security rules. Native IPv6 does not require NAT.
04.decisionCue: Plan prefixes and validate reachability separately.

04.title: Dual-stack rollout and DNS dependency
04.imageBrief: Dual-stack rollout and DNS dependency — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Inventory IPv6 client, service, SDK and DNS dependencies before publishing AAAA records.
Test both address families end to end, verify supported load-balancer/target address modes, monitor and keep rollback.
04.decisionCue: A DNS record does not prove a functioning IPv6 path.

04.title: Egress-only internet gateway for IPv6
04.imageBrief: Egress-only internet gateway for IPv6 — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: An egress-only IGW supports initiated IPv6 internet connections and their responses, blocking unsolicited inbound.
Route ::/0 to the egress-only IGW and retain appropriate IPv6 SG/NACL rules; it performs no NAT.
04.decisionCue: Separate native IPv6 outbound control from IPv4 translation.

04.title: NAT64 and DNS64 for IPv6-only workloads
04.imageBrief: NAT64 and DNS64 for IPv6-only workloads — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: Subnet DNS64 synthesizes AAAA using 64:ff9b::/96 when only IPv4 A is available.
NAT Gateway NAT64 translates application traffic routed to that prefix; public NAT needs IGW for IPv4 internet. Resolver is not a traffic hop.
04.decisionCue: Verify DNS synthesis, translation route and application compatibility.

04.title: IPv6 security controls and logging
04.imageBrief: IPv6 security controls and logging — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.4.
learningNotes: IPv4 rules do not cover IPv6. Audit IPv6 exposure, least privilege source ranges, routing and logs independently.
Support essential ICMPv6 such as path MTU discovery and validate security-stack/service support.
04.decisionCue: Test inbound and outbound in both address families.

04.title: Multi-Region network traffic patterns
04.imageBrief: Multi-Region network traffic patterns — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Route 53 DNS policies include latency, weighted, failover and location-based decisions; TTL/cache affects visibility.
Global Accelerator standard routing uses stable anycast entry addresses and healthy supported endpoints; regional application/data readiness remains essential.
04.decisionCue: Separate global client entry from private backend connectivity.

04.title: Cost-aware connectivity architecture
04.imageBrief: Cost-aware connectivity architecture — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Estimate hourly resources, processed GB, applicable AZ/Region/internet transfer and operational resilience along the actual path.
Compare endpoints, AZ-local NAT and centralized egress. TGW has no separate cross-AZ transfer charge between attachments; surrounding services can charge.
04.decisionCue: Apply current regional pricing to measured traffic volume.

04.title: Scenario: isolated multi-account application
04.imageBrief: Scenario: isolated multi-account application — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Separate TGW route-table association/propagation permits Prod and Dev to reach shared services without direct interconnection.
Use local S3 gateway endpoints and policies per VPC, approved inspected egress, nonoverlap and allowed/denied path tests.
04.decisionCue: Test the access matrix, including forbidden paths.

04.title: Scenario: inspect east-west and outbound traffic
04.imageBrief: Scenario: inspect east-west and outbound traffic — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.3.
learningNotes: Force east-west and outbound traffic through chosen inspection with deliberate routes and symmetric flow handling.
NAT translates IPv4; firewall enforces inspection. Validate logs, endpoint health, return direction, bypass prevention and AZ failure.
04.decisionCue: A direct working route can still violate inspection policy.

04.title: Network architecture decision synthesis
04.imageBrief: Network architecture decision synthesis — an original visual explanation grounded in SAP-C03 skill 1.4.1.
learningNotes: Choose addressing, connectivity, internet access, security and resilience according to requirements and permitted traffic.
Prove identity, DNS, source route, inspection, destination and return path with logs, tests and cost analysis.
04.decisionCue: Explain the architecture choice and its failure/cost tradeoffs.

04.title: NAT instances: operate the forwarding host deliberately
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Configure the complete path: A NAT instance is an EC2 forwarding host in a suitable public subnet. Configure its public/EIP path, forwarding software and private-subnet route, and disable source/destination checking as required. Own the failure handling: Instance bandwidth, security configuration, patching, scaling and failover are your responsibility. A single forwarding host is a single failure domain. Compare managed egress: Use an appropriate managed NAT design when it meets the workload requirements. Do not infer that a legacy NAT-instance example supplies managed availability or automatic scaling.
learningNotes: Configure the complete path: A NAT instance is an EC2 forwarding host in a suitable public subnet. Configure its public/EIP path, forwarding software and private-subnet route, and disable source/destination checking as required.
Own the failure handling: Instance bandwidth, security configuration, patching, scaling and failover are your responsibility. A single forwarding host is a single failure domain.

Compare managed egress: Use an appropriate managed NAT design when it meets the workload requirements. Do not infer that a legacy NAT-instance example supplies managed availability or automatic scaling.
04.decisionCue: A route to a forwarding instance works only when the host and the return path work too.

04.title: Flow Logs: inspect the fields and the observation point
04.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Read the flow record: Interface, source/destination addresses, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, timestamps, action and log status describe an aggregated observed flow, not the application payload. Interpret NAT correctly: At middlebox or NAT interfaces, srcaddr/dstaddr can reflect the observation point. Supported packet-level fields such as pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr help distinguish original packet addresses. Avoid false conclusions: ACCEPT or REJECT is evidence, not a complete root cause. Correlate both directions, security controls, routes and application logs; some traffic is excluded and records can be delayed or skipped.
learningNotes: Read the flow record: Interface, source/destination addresses, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, timestamps, action and log status describe an aggregated observed flow, not the application payload.

Interpret NAT correctly: At middlebox or NAT interfaces, srcaddr/dstaddr can reflect the observation point. Supported packet-level fields such as pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr help distinguish original packet addresses.

Avoid false conclusions: ACCEPT or REJECT is evidence, not a complete root cause. Correlate both directions, security controls, routes and application logs; some traffic is excluded and records can be delayed or skipped.
04.decisionCue: The ENI, field definition and collection scope determine what a flow-log record proves.

05.title: DNS answers a name; routing carries the traffic
05.imageBrief: Separate DNS lookup from application connection; verify TTL, route and security independently.
learningNotes: DNS lookup returns an address; the application connects using separate routes, security and TLS.
TTL caches mean record changes need not be visible immediately.
05.decisionCue: Separate name resolution from application reachability.

05.title: Recursive resolution, authoritative answers and caching
05.imageBrief: Explain stub, recursive and authoritative roles, positive/negative caching and TTL.
learningNotes: Stub clients ask recursive resolvers, which use cache or authoritative DNS.
Positive and negative caching affect answers; changing a record does not flush existing caches.
05.decisionCue: Identify which cache and authority answered.

05.title: Public and private DNS views: split-horizon design
05.imageBrief: Compare public delegation with associated private zones and missing-record behavior.
learningNotes: Public and associated private hosted zones can give different answers for the same name.
A selected matching private zone does not automatically fall back to public DNS for missing names or types.
05.decisionCue: Inspect the client resolver and DNS view.

05.title: VPC DNS attributes, DHCP options and client resolvers
05.imageBrief: Distinguish DNS attributes and custom DNS forwarding; use inbound endpoints for remote resolution.
learningNotes: Inspect DHCP/custom resolver configuration and enableDnsSupport/enableDnsHostnames requirements for private DNS.
Remote clients should query Resolver inbound endpoints, not VPC base+2. Endpoint SGs differ from unfilterable AmazonProvidedDNS traffic.
05.decisionCue: Check client configuration and VPC attributes.

05.title: Private hosted zones and cross-account VPC association
05.imageBrief: Show association authorization, visibility, Profiles/RAM alternatives and routing independence.
learningNotes: Private-zone visibility comes from associations, including direct cross-account authorization/association or supported Profiles mechanisms.
VPC peering/TGW alone does not share the zone. Inbound endpoint VPC must resolve the intended private namespace.
05.decisionCue: Prove association and DNS visibility.

05.title: Namespace precedence, NXDOMAIN and reverse DNS
05.imageBrief: Most-specific zone/rule, same-domain forwarding precedence, no public fallback, PTR/reverse rules.
learningNotes: The most-specific matching private zone wins; same-domain forwarding rules take precedence over private hosted zones.
Missing names/types can yield NXDOMAIN/NODATA without public fallback. PTR uses reverse namespaces and may need supported auto-defined-rule overrides.
05.decisionCue: Check namespace specificity and precedence.

05.title: Inbound Resolver endpoints: on-premises queries into AWS
05.imageBrief: Forward from corporate DNS to resilient inbound endpoint IPs; associate relevant private zones.
learningNotes: Corporate DNS forwards AWS private suffixes to resilient inbound endpoint IPs over private connectivity.
Endpoint VPC zone visibility, DNS settings, UDP/TCP53, routes and response paths must all be correct.
05.decisionCue: Inbound queries enter AWS Resolver.

05.title: Outbound Resolver endpoints and conditional forwarding
05.imageBrief: Associate suffix-specific rules to client VPCs; route endpoint traffic to corporate DNS.
learningNotes: Associated suffix rules send AWS queries through an outbound endpoint to target corporate DNS IPs.
Most-specific rules and reverse namespaces matter; endpoint-to-target routes/security and return paths must work.
05.decisionCue: Outbound queries leave AWS Resolver toward corporate DNS.

05.title: Bidirectional hybrid DNS without forwarding loops
05.imageBrief: Separate namespace authority, forwarding and supported delegation; avoid looping catch-all rules.
learningNotes: Assign distinct AWS and corporate namespace authority and forward each suffix toward its owner.
Avoid sending the same suffix back and forth. Supported Resolver delegation modes differ from simple conditional forwarding.
05.decisionCue: Give each suffix one authoritative owner.

05.title: Resolver endpoint security, capacity and AZ resilience
05.imageBrief: UDP/TCP 53, stateful SG/stateless NACL response paths, multi-AZ IPs, capacity and health.
learningNotes: Inbound endpoint SG permits DNS from forwarders; outbound endpoint SG permits DNS to target servers. Stateful return is tracked.
NACL query/ephemeral response paths, TCP/UDP53, multi-AZ endpoint IPs, target redundancy and capacity monitoring are separate requirements.
05.decisionCue: Test both DNS transports and AZ failure.

05.title: Share Resolver rules across accounts with AWS RAM
05.imageBrief: Central rule ownership and consumer associations; connectivity and authorization remain distinct.
learningNotes: The network account can share forwarding rules using AWS RAM; workload VPCs associate them and use the owner endpoint.
Sharing does not grant private-zone visibility or app connectivity. Endpoint-to-target routes and security remain required.
05.decisionCue: Share policy with explicit consumer association.

05.title: Route 53 Profiles for consistent multi-VPC DNS
05.imageBrief: Bundle supported zone/rule/DNS Firewall associations and distribute with RAM; regional scope and precedence.
learningNotes: Regional Route 53 Profiles bundle supported private-zone associations, Resolver rules, DNS Firewall, logging and DNS settings for VPCs/accounts.
Local associations/settings can take precedence. PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint DNS integration is distinct from Resolver endpoints.
05.decisionCue: Verify effective configuration per VPC.

05.title: Resolve PrivateLink service names from hybrid networks
05.imageBrief: Private DNS, inbound endpoint forwarding, endpoint reachability and security; avoid application IP hardcoding.
learningNotes: Hybrid clients resolve configured service private DNS through an inbound endpoint, then connect separately to the interface endpoint private IP.
Check DNS view, VPN/DX routes, endpoint SG/service port and provider service state; avoid hardcoded ENI addresses.
05.decisionCue: Resolve privately, then validate the connection.

05.title: DNS Firewall: domain filtering and policy evaluation
05.imageBrief: Domain lists, priority/actions, alerts and failure behavior; DNS policy differs from packet inspection.
learningNotes: DNS Firewall evaluates lower numeric association/rule priorities first; ALLOW/BLOCK terminate matching evaluation while ALERT continues.
Default failure mode is closed. Query logs reveal decisions; DNS filtering does not replace egress controls or inspect all third-party encrypted DNS.
05.decisionCue: Use DNS filtering with network egress controls.

05.title: Resolver query logs and DNS observability
05.imageBrief: Query metadata, destinations, limits/cache effects, logging policy and troubleshooting correlation.
learningNotes: Regional Resolver query logging can send data to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose; confirm association and destination permissions.
Cached responses are not logged as new unique queries. Public-zone query logging is separate, and DNS logs are not packet capture.
05.decisionCue: Correlate logs with cache and client behavior.

05.title: Alias, CNAME, apex records and delegation
05.imageBrief: Use supported alias targets, CNAME constraints and public delegation; private delegation is separate.
learningNotes: Alias supports eligible AWS targets/same-zone records and zone-apex use subject to target/type constraints; CNAME maps to another DNS name and cannot be apex.
NS delegation changes authoritative ownership of a subdomain. Same-zone alias type must match its target record; ALB aliases use supported A/AAAA.
05.decisionCue: Choose record shape and authority separately.

05.title: DNS health checks and private application failover
05.imageBrief: Public checker reachability, CloudWatch-alarm health checks, alias target health and readiness limits.
learningNotes: Public Route 53 health checkers cannot directly probe private IPs; private failover can use metric/alarm-data-stream health checks or supported target health.
SetAlarmState does not force health-check state. Test readiness, missing data, all-unhealthy behavior, capacity and caching.
05.decisionCue: Use a reachable and meaningful health signal.

05.title: Route 53 routing policies, TTL and controlled shifts
05.imageBrief: Latency/weighted/failover/location policy decisions and health evaluation; cache affects visibility.
learningNotes: Choose simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity or multivalue according to the required decision and supported zone/record scope.
IP-based routing additionally uses configured client CIDR collections where supported. Weights affect DNS answers, not exact request percentages; TTL and health behavior matter.
05.decisionCue: Choose routing behavior, then account for caching.

05.title: Multi-Region private DNS and Resolver architecture
05.imageBrief: Regional endpoints/rules, zone associations and resilience; private backend connectivity and client entry.
learningNotes: A private hosted zone can associate VPCs across Regions; Resolver endpoints, rules, Profiles and hybrid paths are regional dependencies.
Deploy regional resilience explicitly, test cached answers and avoid unintended central-Region dependency.
05.decisionCue: Treat regional DNS paths as regional dependencies.

05.title: DNSSEC signing versus Resolver validation
05.imageBrief: Public-zone signing and chain of trust vs query validation; private scope limitations and SERVFAIL.
learningNotes: Public-zone signing and Resolver validation are distinct: KSK signs DNSKEY record set; ZSK signs zone record sets, with parent DS establishing trust.
DNSSEC authenticates/integrity-checks DNS, not encryption. Broken chains can cause SERVFAIL; monitor KMS/signing and plan safe rollover.
05.decisionCue: Validate the full DNSSEC chain of trust.

05.title: Troubleshoot timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL
05.imageBrief: Use caller/resolver/zone/rule/cache/log evidence; isolate security, DNSSEC and forwarding faults.
learningNotes: Use timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL as evidence with multiple possible causes.
Reproduce same caller/resolver/type; inspect effective zone/rule, cache, DNSSEC, firewall and upstream logs before changing routes.
05.decisionCue: Reproduce the exact caller, resolver and type.

05.title: Scenario: resilient multi-account hybrid DNS
05.imageBrief: Apply namespaces, zones, inbound/outbound rules, shared policy, logging, failure tests and cost tradeoffs.
learningNotes: Design distinct namespaces, regional inbound/outbound endpoints, private-zone/Profiles associations and shared suffix rules for each client view.
Validate DNS and app connectivity separately, including logs, policy, loop prevention, endpoint/AZ/Region failure and cost/retention.
05.decisionCue: Test both directions and every client view.

05.title: IP-based routing and geoproximity answer different questions
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Route by client CIDR: IP-based records use CIDR collections and location mappings for known client network ranges. Configure the supported unmatched-location behavior and consider DNS resolver/client-subnet visibility. Shift geographic catchments: Geoproximity uses resource/user location and a bias to expand or shrink the area served by an endpoint. It is different from country-based geolocation and measured-latency routing. Choose the control surface: Current geoproximity records can be configured directly where supported; Traffic Flow is useful for complex reusable policies. Do not repeat the older claim that every geoproximity configuration requires Traffic Flow.
learningNotes: Route by client CIDR: IP-based records use CIDR collections and location mappings for known client network ranges. Configure the supported unmatched-location behavior and consider DNS resolver/client-subnet visibility.

Shift geographic catchments: Geoproximity uses resource/user location and a bias to expand or shrink the area served by an endpoint. It is different from country-based geolocation and measured-latency routing.

Choose the control surface: Current geoproximity records can be configured directly where supported; Traffic Flow is useful for complex reusable policies. Do not repeat the older claim that every geoproximity configuration requires Traffic Flow.
05.decisionCue: Client networks, user geography and measured latency are different routing inputs.

05.title: Health checks: endpoint probes, aggregation and private signals
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Check a public endpoint: HTTP/HTTPS checks evaluate configured response criteria; TCP checks test connection behavior. Allow checker traffic, use the intended hostname/path, and validate optional response-string matching. Combine health evidence: Calculated checks combine child results using configured thresholds or logical rules. Checker aggregation and calculated-child limits are separate controls; consult current API/console limits. Monitor private readiness: Public health checkers cannot directly reach private endpoints. Use supported CloudWatch metric/alarm health signals and a prepared failover target; changing an alarm's display state is not a substitute for its metric data.
learningNotes: Check a public endpoint: HTTP/HTTPS checks evaluate configured response criteria; TCP checks test connection behavior. Allow checker traffic, use the intended hostname/path, and validate optional response-string matching.

Combine health evidence: Calculated checks combine child results using configured thresholds or logical rules. Checker aggregation and calculated-child limits are separate controls; consult current API/console limits.

Monitor private readiness: Public health checkers cannot directly reach private endpoints. Use supported CloudWatch metric/alarm health signals and a prepared failover target; changing an alarm's display state is not a substitute for its metric data.
05.decisionCue: A health check must measure the failure your routing policy is intended to handle.

05.title: Traffic Flow and DNS caching make controlled changes repeatable
05.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Build reusable routing logic: Traffic Flow represents complex decision trees as versioned traffic policies and policy instances. A policy definition and the DNS records created from it are different resources. Test geographic and weighted decisions: Bias changes catchment size, while weights influence DNS-answer selection. Neither guarantees an exact share of individual HTTP requests because resolvers and clients cache answers. Plan rollout and rollback: Review TTL, record scope, health behavior, cost and the fallback for all-unhealthy or unmatched locations. Validate authoritative answers and client behavior before broad rollout.
learningNotes: Build reusable routing logic: Traffic Flow represents complex decision trees as versioned traffic policies and policy instances. A policy definition and the DNS records created from it are different resources.

Test geographic and weighted decisions: Bias changes catchment size, while weights influence DNS-answer selection. Neither guarantees an exact share of individual HTTP requests because resolvers and clients cache answers.

Plan rollout and rollback: Review TTL, record scope, health behavior, cost and the fallback for all-unhealthy or unmatched locations. Validate authoritative answers and client behavior before broad rollout.
05.decisionCue: Version the routing decision and test the cached client path, not just the policy editor.

06.title: Hybrid design starts with requirements
06.imageBrief: Hybrid design starts with requirements: Measure latency and jitter, steady and burst bandwidth, migration windows and critical backup capacity before selecting transport. Define encryption endpoints, acceptable interruption, operational effort and cost. Check shared devices, providers, circuits, power and sites.
learningNotes: Measure latency and jitter, steady and burst bandwidth, migration windows and critical backup capacity before selecting transport.
Define encryption endpoints, acceptable interruption, operational effort and cost. Check shared devices, providers, circuits, power and sites.
06.decisionCue: Measure latency and jitter, steady and burst bandwidth, migration windows and critical backup capacity before selecting transport.

06.title: VPN and Direct Connect: choose the transport
06.imageBrief: VPN and Direct Connect: choose the transport: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned. IPsec protects between VPN endpoints; application TLS can extend protection beyond them. Test backup throughput and convergence under representative load.
learningNotes: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned.
IPsec protects between VPN endpoints; application TLS can extend protection beyond them. Test backup throughput and convergence under representative load.
06.decisionCue: VPN provides IPsec over a supported transport; Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path whose delivery must be provisioned.

06.title: Two VPN tunnels, one customer-device risk
06.imageBrief: Two VPN tunnels, one customer-device risk: Each VPN connection has two AWS-side tunnels. Configure both; one customer appliance, ISP or site can still be a shared failure. Add a separate connection with independent equipment and dependencies. Measure route convergence and real application recovery separately.
learningNotes: Each VPN connection has two AWS-side tunnels. Configure both; one customer appliance, ISP or site can still be a shared failure.
Add a separate connection with independent equipment and dependencies. Measure route convergence and real application recovery separately.
06.decisionCue: Each VPN connection has two AWS-side tunnels. Configure both; one customer appliance, ISP or site can still be a shared failure.

06.title: VGW or Transit Gateway: choose the scope
06.imageBrief: VGW or Transit Gateway: choose the scope: A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and does not support VPN ECMP; Transit Gateway serves a broader routed network. Gateway selection does not replace subnet routes, return routes, segmentation, security groups or resilience testing.
learningNotes: A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and does not support VPN ECMP; Transit Gateway serves a broader routed network.
Gateway selection does not replace subnet routes, return routes, segmentation, security groups or resilience testing.
06.decisionCue: A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and does not support VPN ECMP; Transit Gateway serves a broader routed network.

06.title: BGP, route propagation and return paths
06.imageBrief: BGP, route propagation and return paths: Static and dynamic BGP routing support depends on gateway type. Configure both AWS subnet routes and customer-side routes. TGW association selects the ingress attachment route table; propagation installs learned prefixes into selected tables. A learned route alone does not establish the entire return path.
learningNotes: Static and dynamic BGP routing support depends on gateway type. Configure both AWS subnet routes and customer-side routes.
TGW association selects the ingress attachment route table; propagation installs learned prefixes into selected tables. A learned route alone does not establish the entire return path.
06.decisionCue: Static and dynamic BGP routing support depends on gateway type. Configure both AWS subnet routes and customer-side routes.

06.title: VPN throughput, ECMP and acceleration
06.imageBrief: VPN throughput, ECMP and acceleration: Standard VPN tunnels support up to 1.25 Gbps; supported Large Bandwidth Tunnels support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN. Large Bandwidth Tunnels do not support acceleration. VPN ECMP requires dynamic routing; aggregate throughput does not give one flow the sum of all paths.
learningNotes: Standard VPN tunnels support up to 1.25 Gbps; supported Large Bandwidth Tunnels support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN.
Large Bandwidth Tunnels do not support acceleration. VPN ECMP requires dynamic routing; aggregate throughput does not give one flow the sum of all paths.
06.decisionCue: Standard VPN tunnels support up to 1.25 Gbps; supported Large Bandwidth Tunnels support up to 5 Gbps per tunnel on Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN.

06.title: Direct Connect: physical link to BGP session
06.imageBrief: Direct Connect: physical link to BGP session
learningNotes: An AWS port dedicated to you; arrange carrier delivery and the facility cross-connect using the LOA-CFA.
A Direct Connect Partner provides a share of its connection. Accept it in your account.
50–500 Mbps options; 1, 2, 5, 10 or 25 Gbps. Availability varies by partner and location.
Customer router and last mile • facility cross-connect • AWS port • partner delivery, when hosted.
Commission separately: physical link • VLAN and VIF • BGP • application and return path.
06.decisionCue: Lead time is provider-dependent. A physical UP state is not proof of application access.

06.title: Private, public and transit virtual interfaces
06.imageBrief: Private, public and transit virtual interfaces: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements. Private VIF/VGW and transit VIF/TGW designs use different gateway association models. BGP authentication does not encrypt application data.
learningNotes: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements.
Private VIF/VGW and transit VIF/TGW designs use different gateway association models. BGP authentication does not encrypt application data.
06.decisionCue: Public VIFs reach AWS public prefixes, not arbitrary internet destinations; comply with addressing and prefix ownership requirements.

06.title: Direct Connect gateway: associations and allowed prefixes
06.imageBrief: Direct Connect gateway: associations and allowed prefixes: With VGW associations, allowed prefixes filter entire VPC CIDRs; a wider range does not synthesize an advertised summary. With TGW associations, configured allowed prefixes are originated from the Direct Connect gateway ASN. Avoid overlapping allowed prefixes across its TGW associations and validate actual downstream reachability.
learningNotes: With VGW associations, allowed prefixes filter entire VPC CIDRs; a wider range does not synthesize an advertised summary.

With TGW associations, configured allowed prefixes are originated from the Direct Connect gateway ASN. Avoid overlapping allowed prefixes across its TGW associations and validate actual downstream reachability.
06.decisionCue: With VGW associations, allowed prefixes filter entire VPC CIDRs; a wider range does not synthesize an advertised summary.

06.title: Hybrid hub: Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway
06.imageBrief: Hybrid hub: Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability. Configure VPC subnet routes and on-premises return routes. Shared connectivity does not mean every attachment should communicate; validate each Region independently.
learningNotes: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability.

06.decisionCue: The transit VIF provides transport and BGP; the Direct Connect gateway supplies associations and allowed advertisements; TGW route tables select downstream reachability.

06.title: BGP policy: choose each direction
06.imageBrief: Two independent preferences
learningNotes: Your router controls traffic toward AWS; AWS selects paths toward your advertised networks.
For equal-length prefixes on private and transit VIFs, supported local-preference communities influence AWS path choice.
Use AS-path policy carefully; longest-prefix matching can override a less-specific backup.
Test both directions and failover; do not assume symmetry.
06.decisionCue: Two independent preferences

06.title: Direct Connect resilience: separate failure domains
06.imageBrief: Diversity is the design
learningNotes: Separate customer routers, power and access circuits.
Use independent AWS devices and multiple Direct Connect locations for location-failure protection.
A second circuit through the same provider conduit may share the same failure.
Test loss of a device, circuit and location; validate surviving capacity.
06.decisionCue: Diversity is the design

06.title: LAG: more capacity is not location diversity
06.imageBrief: One logical interface
learningNotes: Dedicated connections, same port speed, same Direct Connect endpoint. All members operate active/active.
The LAG goes down when live members fall below the configured threshold. Protect remaining links from overload.
Traffic is distributed across members. One flow is not guaranteed the sum of all link speeds.
06.decisionCue: LAG shares an endpoint failure domain. Use independent devices and locations for resilience.

06.title: Direct Connect backup: design the degraded mode
06.imageBrief: Failure is a workload event
learningNotes: Use independent Direct Connect paths or an internet VPN backup according to requirements.
Advertise and select routes deliberately; a more-specific route can defeat the intended primary path.
Size backup throughput for critical workloads and defer noncritical transfers if needed.
Measure route convergence, application reconnection and recovery during a real failover test.
06.decisionCue: Failure is a workload event

06.title: Encryption: identify the protected boundary
06.imageBrief: Transport and protection differ
learningNotes: TLS protects application sessions between their TLS endpoints.
IPsec protects routed traffic between VPN tunnel endpoints, including supported VPN-over-Direct-Connect designs.
MACsec provides point-to-point Layer2 protection on supported Direct Connect links; it is not application end-to-end encryption.
Direct Connect is not encrypted by default. Select protection for the actual compliance boundary.
06.decisionCue: Transport and protection differ

06.title: Private IP VPN: encrypted overlay on private transport
06.imageBrief: An overlay still needs an underlay
learningNotes: Private IP Site-to-Site VPN can run over Direct Connect using a transit VIF, Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway.
The VPN endpoints use private addressing; the IPsec tunnels carry protected application traffic.
Underlay reachability and overlay route advertisements have distinct jobs.
Avoid recursive routing and verify VPN capacity, feature compatibility and failover.
06.decisionCue: An overlay still needs an underlay

06.title: Transit Gateway Connect: integrate SD-WAN
06.imageBrief: GRE carries traffic; BGP exchanges routes
learningNotes: Connect attachments use a supported transport attachment such as VPC or Direct Connect.
Connect peers use GRE tunnels and BGP for appliance integration.
GRE does not provide encryption. Protect the transport separately when required.
Plan multiple peers, appliance resilience and routes in both directions.
06.decisionCue: GRE carries traffic; BGP exchanges routes

06.title: Hybrid operations: prove the complete path
06.imageBrief: Troubleshoot by layer
learningNotes: Check physical link, VIF, BGP session and prefix visibility before application policy.
Inspect VPN tunnel metrics and logs, route tables, flow logs and customer-device counters.
Small packets working while large transfers stall can indicate MTU or MSS problems.
Test realistic workloads during failover; record convergence, packet loss and recovery.
06.decisionCue: Troubleshoot by layer

06.title: Compute placement: put constraints first
06.imageBrief: Choose location before platform
learningNotes: AWS Regions provide broad managed-service choices and regional resilience options.
Local Zones place supported resources near users while depending on a parent Region.
Outposts place AWS-managed infrastructure in your facility; site readiness and regional connectivity matter.
Customer-managed on-premises compute gives local control with greater operational responsibility.
06.decisionCue: Choose location before platform

06.title: Outposts: local compute with regional ties
06.imageBrief: An extension with dependencies
learningNotes: AWS supplies and manages supported Outposts infrastructure; customers provide site power, space and connectivity.
Run supported AWS workloads near local systems and data.
The service link connects the Outpost to its parent Region for management and service communication.
During disconnects, some existing local workloads continue; regional dependencies and management operations can be impaired.
06.decisionCue: An extension with dependencies

06.title: Outposts racks: two networking roles
06.imageBrief: Service link and local gateway
learningNotes: The service link provides connectivity back to the parent Region and carries the control-plane path.
The local gateway connects rack subnets with the on-premises network.
Configure routing, addressing and BGP with the customer network; verify supported routing modes.
Outposts servers use local network interfaces rather than the rack local gateway model.
06.decisionCue: Service link and local gateway

06.title: Local Zones: nearby resources, regional dependencies
06.imageBrief: Lower latency needs a full path
learningNotes: Enable a supported Local Zone and create a subnet there as an extension of your VPC.
Place supported compute and storage close to users or local systems.
Service availability and instance choices vary by location; validate before designing.
Keep regional services, data paths, failure recovery and cross-zone transfer in the latency and cost model.
06.decisionCue: Lower latency needs a full path

06.title: EKS Anywhere: Kubernetes you operate
06.imageBrief: Local control plane, local responsibility
learningNotes: Run Kubernetes on supported customer-managed infrastructure using EKS Anywhere tooling.
The customer operates control-plane and worker infrastructure, networking, storage, upgrades and backups.
Plan local image registries, identity, DNS and package access for restricted environments.
EKS Anywhere is different from regional EKS with hybrid nodes; their control-plane locations differ.
06.decisionCue: Local control plane, local responsibility

06.title: ECS Anywhere: external hosts, AWS orchestration
06.imageBrief: Separate running tasks from management
learningNotes: Register supported external servers or VMs with Systems Manager and the ECS agent.
Use ECS to manage supported tasks on external capacity; provision and maintain the hosts yourself.
Inbound connectivity, host networking, storage and load balancing need an explicit design.
During connectivity loss, existing tasks may continue; cloud scheduling and management are impaired.
06.decisionCue: Separate running tasks from management

06.title: Disconnected operation: map every dependency
06.imageBrief: Local compute alone is insufficient
learningNotes: Inventory identity, DNS, secrets, registries, databases and external APIs used by the workload.
Classify what continues locally, what degrades and what requires regional connectivity.
Cache or replicate only where semantics, security and staleness limits permit.
Test disconnect and reconnection, including reconciliation, credential expiry and recovery.
06.decisionCue: Local compute alone is insufficient

06.title: Hybrid case: justify the whole design
06.imageBrief: A decision checklist
learningNotes: Requirement: local low-latency processing, resilient AWS connectivity and encrypted sensitive traffic.
Choose local compute by operational ownership and service dependencies; use diverse network paths.
Specify encryption endpoints, routing preferences, backup capacity and access controls.
Prove application recovery with device, circuit and regional-dependency failures; document tradeoffs.
06.decisionCue: A decision checklist

06.title: VPN CloudHub: connect remote sites
06.imageBrief: A distinct hub-and-spoke option
learningNotes: Multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections can share a virtual private gateway to connect remote sites.
Use BGP with unique customer ASNs and nonoverlapping site prefixes.
The virtual private gateway can re-advertise site routes to other sites.
This is remote-site connectivity, not transitive VPC peering. Compare with Transit Gateway as the network grows.
06.decisionCue: A distinct hub-and-spoke option

06.title: Client VPN: identity, routes and authorization
06.imageBrief: User access needs every control
learningNotes: Authenticate users with a supported method: mutual certificates, Active Directory or federated SAML.
Authorization rules specify destination access; authentication alone does not grant network reachability.
Configure target-network connectivity, endpoint routes and destination security controls.
Plan client addressing, DNS, connection logging and highly available target connectivity.
06.decisionCue: User access needs every control

06.title: Client VPN: choose the traffic path
06.imageBrief: Split tunnel versus full tunnel
learningNotes: Split tunnel installs endpoint routes on the client; matching traffic uses the VPN.
Full tunnel sends client traffic through the VPN; provide a deliberate internet-egress design.
Reach peered VPCs or on-premises networks only with complete routes, authorization and return connectivity.
Transit Gateway integration is supported; check its endpoint-specific requirements and authorization limitations.
06.decisionCue: Split tunnel versus full tunnel

06.title: Direct Connect SiteLink: site-to-site transport
06.imageBrief: Between Direct Connect locations
learningNotes: SiteLink enables supported on-premises sites to exchange traffic through Direct Connect locations.
Enable SiteLink on supported private or transit VIFs associated with the same Direct Connect gateway.
The site-to-site path can bypass AWS Regions; compare route policy and WAN requirements.
SiteLink does not remove customer access-circuit failures or provide automatic end-to-end application encryption.
06.decisionCue: Between Direct Connect locations

06.title: Shared services: replicas, proxies or transit?
06.imageBrief: Three beautiful dimensional vignettes, replicated database blocks, a proxy service desk, and a routing hub. Explanation cards paired with each, navy cyan purple amber. Replicate the service Place application or data replicas in a shared-services VPC. Consumers access those local endpoints. Trade-off: replication lag, consistency, licensing and operating cost. Proxy the application A proxy terminates the consumer connection and opens a separate connection to the on-premises service. Trade-off: proxy scaling, availability, authentication and protocol support. Route through a transit hub Use Transit Gateway when workloads need routed access to on-premises networks; define isolation and return routes. Peering limitation VPC peering cannot provide transit through a peer's VPN or Direct Connect connection. Remember: A replica serves a local copy; a proxy creates a new connection; a transit gateway forwards routed traffic.

06.title: Hybrid internet egress: gateway choice matters

TGW option Transit Gateway supports centralized egress through an egress VPC. Route through a public NAT gateway and an internet gateway. Alternative: on-premises egress VPC traffic can use VPN or Direct Connect to reach an on-premises firewall/NAT. Customer equipment supplies internet egress. Remember: A private NAT gateway cannot provide internet access through an internet gateway.

The public VIF provides AWS public-prefix reachability; it is not general internet transit. Private-IP VPN over Direct Connect Use a transit VIF, Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway for private-IP VPN endpoints. This design uses private addressing for the VPN transport; it is different from a public VIF design. Both need an underlay and an overlay The Direct Connect path carries the encrypted tunnel. VPN routes and return paths carry the application networks. Remember: Direct Connect is not encrypted by default. IPsec adds encryption; it does not remove tunnel capacity limits.

Same destination, different question Two connections advertising the same prefix do not automatically provide equal-cost load sharing on a virtual private gateway. Failure and application recovery Use independent customer devices and circuits. Test route withdrawal, alternate reachability and stateful firewall behavior. 07.title: EC2 lifecycle: know what survives
07.imageBrief: Memory, storage and identity have different lifetimes

Termination removes the instance. EBS retention depends on delete-on-termination settings; protect important data separately.

07.title: Repeatable launches: build a replacement, not a pet

07.title: Tenancy: isolation, licensing and host affinity

07.title: Placement groups: locality, isolation and operational limits
07.imageBrief: Three rich conceptual hardware vignettes, cluster, rack spread and partition replicas. No exact rack topology. A short operation ribbon below. Cluster • performance Supported instances close together in one AZ for low latency and throughput. One rack is not guaranteed; the slower instance limits the pair. Spread • small critical fleets Rack-level spread separates underlying hardware: up to 7 running instances per AZ per group. It can span AZs; host-level spread is an Outposts option. Partition • distributed replicas Up to 7 partitions per AZ, each holding many instances; total capacity is quota-limited. Different partitions do not share racks. Use partition metadata to separate replicas, as in Kafka, Cassandra or HDFS. Change placement deliberately Stop the instance, change placement with ModifyInstancePlacement, then start. Compatible capacity is required; launches or starts can fail when unavailable. Remember: Placement controls locality or hardware separation. It does not create replication or Multi-AZ recovery.

07.title: Auto Scaling groups: define the safe operating range

07.title: Target tracking: choose demand per unit of capacity

Match the metric CPU for CPU-bound work; ALB requests per target for balanced request processing; average network bytes in or out for suitable network-bound workloads. Custom metrics need useful units A queue's raw length is not proportional utilization. Backlog per worker can express demand; choose the target from acceptable latency and processing time. Coordinate readiness and policies Allow instance warmup and verify scale-in. With multiple target tracking policies, any can request scale-out; all scale-in-enabled policies must agree before scale-in. Remember: A scaling metric must describe the bottleneck that more healthy capacity can actually relieve.

07.title: Step scaling: react to the size of the breach
07.imageBrief: Alarm-driven adjustments need tuning

07.title: Scheduled and predictive scaling: prepare ahead
07.imageBrief: Known events and forecast demand are different

07.title: Warmup and warm pools: readiness is not one timer

07.title: Lifecycle hooks: make transitions deliberate
07.imageBrief: A bounded wait gives automation time

07.title: Health checks: identify the failure before replacement

Recovery is a different action Supported EC2 recovery addresses certain system failures; ASG replacement creates new compute. Neither repairs every application or shared dependency. Remember: A healthy guest is not proof of a healthy application. Choose the check and response for the failure domain.

07.title: Scale-in: protect work, not just instance count

07.title: Mixed instances: capacity units must mean the same thing

07.title: EC2 architecture case: prove the bottleneck and recovery

07.title: Precision time: placement for clock accuracy

07.title: HPC storage: choose the access pattern and durability

07.title: Auto Scaling processes: nine controls with different jobs

07.title: Suspended processes: diagnose the side effects

ReplaceUnhealthy can still terminate unhealthy instances without launching replacements. ReplaceUnhealthy suspended Managed health checks can still mark instances unhealthy, but replacement waits until the process resumes. AddToLoadBalancer suspended New instances can launch without registration. Resuming does not register those missed instances automatically; register them explicitly. ScheduledActions suspended Actions scheduled during the suspension are skipped. Resuming does not replay missed schedules. Before resuming Inspect capacity, health, registration and pending work. Resumption may trigger replacement or rebalancing; restore controls deliberately. Remember: Suspending Terminate does not prevent the Spot service from interrupting Spot instances.

08.title: Health checks measure application readiness

Read the reason code Separate timeout, response-code mismatch, failed health check and unused target states before changing infrastructure. Avoid a shared outage cascade A probe that fails whenever a shared dependency fails can remove every target at once. Design readiness checks deliberately. 08.title: ALB routes by the request's meaning
08.imageBrief: Glossy request envelope with four readable decision cards, different composition from previous slides. Match the request Conditions include host, path, HTTP headers, request method, query strings and source IP. Order specific rules before broad matches. Choose the response Forward to target groups, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, or return a fixed response. The default rule handles unmatched requests. Use the protocol features ALB supports HTTP/2 and WebSocket upgrades. After an upgrade, messages use the established connection to the selected target. Example decision Requests for shop.example.com and /checkout can reach the checkout service; /catalog can reach another group without another public ALB. 08.title: ALB targets: instances, IPs and functions

Fargate and awsvpc Tasks have their own network interfaces and private addresses. Use IP target groups rather than registering the host instance. 08.title: TLS termination: identify both connections

HTTPS encrypts the backend leg; ALB does not validate the target certificate. Client certificates ALB mTLS verify authenticates client certificates against a trust store. In mTLS passthrough mode, certificate details go to the application in HTTP headers. 08.title: Authenticate users, then authorize actions

08.title: Choose how ALB distributes requests
08.imageBrief: Four large polished concept tiles with evenly sized readable text; use no data chart. Least outstanding requests Prefers targets with fewer in-progress requests. Useful when request duration or processing capability varies. Weighted random Random distribution with optional Automatic Target Weights anomaly mitigation. It cannot be combined with stickiness or slow start. 08.title: Drain connections before removing capacity
08.imageBrief: Four staggered glossy lifecycle cards; no precise flowchart. Deregister safely A deregistering target enters draining. Know the timer For ALB instance and IP targets, deregistration delay defaults to 300 seconds and can be configured from 0 to 3600 seconds. Coordinate the application Align container or process shutdown grace, long requests and connection handling. Terminating the process early can still break requests. Roll out in stages Start replacement capacity, wait for readiness, shift traffic, drain old targets and then terminate. Health and rollback checks belong in the deployment. 08.title: Weighted target groups enable controlled releases
08.imageBrief: Two glossy release-version pedestals, amber control dial and four concise explanatory cards, no numeric chart. Account for stickiness Group-level stickiness can keep a client in the selected group. Existing sessions may not immediately follow a changed weight. Do not assume automatic failover If a weighted group is empty or unhealthy, ALB does not automatically move its assigned traffic to another healthy group. Make rollback practical Observe errors, latency and business outcomes. Restore weights when needed; schema and data compatibility require their own rollback plan. Remember: Weighted forwarding controls traffic share; deployment safety requires health signals and compatible state.

08.title: NLB keeps flows together and checks health

09.title: Encryption: protect data and authorize the key

SSE-S3 and KMS-based options have different key-management, authorization and audit implications. KMS permissions matter An S3 permission alone can be insufficient for KMS-encrypted objects. Validate the relevant KMS key policy, IAM permissions and regional key availability. Protect transport too Use HTTPS and appropriate bucket-policy conditions. Plan key access for replication, cross-account readers and recovery rather than only the writer. Remember: Encryption is useful only when authorized applications can use the keys and unauthorized callers cannot.

09.title: Versioning preserves object history
09.imageBrief: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples. Keep distinct versions Versioning preserves prior versions when a key is overwritten. Deleting without a version ID usually adds a delete marker rather than erasing all history. Recover deliberately Recover the required version or remove the appropriate delete marker. Permanently deleting a particular version removes that stored version. Manage the accumulated cost Noncurrent versions and delete markers need deliberate lifecycle rules. Suspending versioning is not the same as deleting historical versions. Remember: Versioning creates recovery options; lifecycle and permissions determine whether they remain useful.

09.title: Object Lock: retention and legal hold

Use version-level protection Object Lock protects eligible object versions in a versioned bucket. A legal hold is separate from a time-based retention period. Governance mode Appropriately authorized callers can bypass governance retention when they explicitly request that operation. Compliance mode Protected versions cannot be deleted or have retention shortened before expiry, including by the account root user. Remember: Choose retention mode, duration and recovery procedures before applying irreversible protection.

09.title: Serve private static objects through CloudFront

The application can keep its dynamic compute separately. Protect the origin For a supported S3 bucket origin, use Origin Access Control and the appropriate bucket policy to restrict direct origin access. Choose the endpoint deliberately An S3 website endpoint and a regular S3 bucket origin have different capabilities. Viewer HTTPS and origin access must match the chosen design. Remember: A CDN improves delivery; it does not automatically make an exposed bucket private.

09.title: Online storage classes: availability and recovery tradeoffs

Account for retrieval charges, minimum duration and minimum billable size. One Zone-IA Infrequent-access data in one AZ. Use when the data can be recreated or another recoverable copy exists; it does not tolerate loss of that AZ. Remember: Durability design, availability, retrieval charges and AZ failure tolerance are different dimensions.

09.title: Glacier classes: choose retrieval behavior

Glacier Flexible Retrieval Asynchronous restore supports different retrieval tiers. Plan the restoration delay, temporary restored copy and retrieval charges. Glacier Deep Archive Long-retention data with a longer recovery lead time. A cheaper stored copy may be unsuitable for a short recovery objective. Remember: Archive selection must satisfy the time needed to restore usable data, not just the storage price.

09.title: Intelligent-Tiering follows changing access

Separate online and optional archive tiers Optional Archive Access starts after at least 90 days without access; Deep Archive Access after at least 180 days. Both require a restore before reading. Include the overhead Monitoring and automation charges apply to eligible objects. Objects below 128 KB stay in Frequent Access and are not monitored or charged the monitoring fee. Remember: Intelligent-Tiering optimizes access-tier placement; it does not decide whether an object should exist.

09.title: Lifecycle rules manage the whole object history

Transition with intent Rules can move eligible objects to supported storage classes or expire them. Filter the intended key prefixes or tags and validate transition constraints. 09.title: Replication timing, existing objects and deletion

Monitor replication delay and failures. Its SLA starts service credits below a 99.9% monthly 15-minute replication percentage, subject to terms. Permanent version deletion and all source-side operations do not automatically become equivalent destination actions. Remember: Asynchronous replication has a recovery-point implication and is not a substitute for independent retention.

09.title: S3 event notifications: react without coupling

Select the destination Supported direct destinations include Lambda, standard SQS queues and standard SNS topics. Permissions and regional compatibility must be correct. 09.title: EventBridge adds richer event routing

09.title: Scale requests across useful key prefixes

Observe the real bottleneck Handle transient throttling with retries and backoff. Client capacity, network throughput and KMS request quotas can constrain the complete system. 09.title: Multipart upload: parallelize and retry parts

09.title: Multi-Region Access Points: global entry and regional data
