Choose application-managed caching: ElastiCache can hold aggregates, rendered results, sessions and other application-defined values. The application owns serialization, keys and refresh logic.
Account for the work: Neither choice removes IAM, network, capacity or failure planning. A computed aggregate in a cache needs a correct invalidation or rebuild path.

11.title: Cache-aside makes the miss path part of the architecture
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Read the cache first: The application looks up a stable cache key. A valid hit can avoid a database read and reduce latency. Fill on a miss: On a miss, read the authoritative database, then store an appropriate value with an expiry policy. The application still returns the database result. Keep the database protected: Concurrent misses can cause a stampede. Use suitable request coalescing, bounded retries, jitter or other controls and monitor hit rate and database load.

Fill on a miss: On a miss, read the authoritative database, then store an appropriate value with an expiry policy. The application still returns the database result.
Keep the database protected: Concurrent misses can cause a stampede. Use suitable request coalescing, bounded retries, jitter or other controls and monitor hit rate and database load.
11.decisionCue: A cache that misses safely is more useful than one with a pretty hit path.

11.title: Cache invalidation connects writes to future reads
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose a write strategy: A database update can invalidate a cached value or refresh it through an application-controlled write path. Define the ordering and failure behavior. Use TTL as a bound: Expiration limits how long some stale data may remain, but cannot guarantee immediate correctness after every write. Sensitive workflows may need source reads. Handle races: A slow reader can refill old data after an invalidation. Versioned keys, conditional updates or suitable coordination can prevent stale resurrection.

Use TTL as a bound: Expiration limits how long some stale data may remain, but cannot guarantee immediate correctness after every write. Sensitive workflows may need source reads.
Handle races: A slow reader can refill old data after an invalidation. Versioned keys, conditional updates or suitable coordination can prevent stale resurrection.
11.decisionCue: Cache correctness depends on ordering as well as expiry.

11.title: A shared session store helps application instances stay replaceable
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Write session state centrally: After authentication, store the required session state with a suitable identifier and expiry. Keep credentials and tokens protected. Read from any instance: Another application instance retrieves the same authorized session. Load-balancer stickiness is no longer the only way to reach that state. Plan loss and expiry: Cache eviction, failover or expiration can end sessions. Define acceptable reauthentication behavior and secure transport, access and cookie settings.

11.title: Compare cache engines and deployment models separately
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Valkey or Redis OSS: Supported deployments provide rich data structures, replication, snapshots and failover capabilities. Verify the exact engine/version and operating mode. Node-based Memcached: Traditional Memcached nodes shard disposable data and use a multithreaded engine. They do not inherit Redis replication or snapshot behavior. Current serverless differences: Serverless Memcached supports snapshots, so the PDF's blanket no-backup statement is too broad. Managed ElastiCache also should not be described as providing generic Redis AOF durability.

11.title: Replication, sharding and persistence solve different cache risks
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Shard for capacity: Distribute keys across shards to spread memory and request load. Hot keys and uneven key distribution can still constrain a shard. Replicate for availability: Supported Valkey/Redis deployments use replicas and Multi-AZ automatic failover. Reader traffic may see replication lag. Recover deliberate state: Snapshots and tested restore procedures protect eligible cache data. Replication is not a backup, and persistence support depends on the selected deployment.

11.title: Find the limiting layer during an extreme-rate event
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Trace the complete request: Edge caches, API throttles, compute concurrency, connection pools, database partitions and encryption APIs can each constrain the path. Measure demand units: Requests per second, concurrent work, I/O size and cache hit rate are different quantities. A fast cache does not fix an overloaded write path. Use current quotas: The PDF's combined rate chart contains historical defaults and simplifications. Confirm Region/account quotas, burst behavior and service-specific limits instead of treating any layer as unlimited.

11.title: OpenSearch is a search index with a chosen operating model
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the search use case: Full-text search, log analytics, clickstream exploration and security analysis benefit from indexed documents and suitable mappings. Select managed or serverless: Managed domains expose cluster capacity choices. Serverless collections use a different capacity and security model; confirm workload and feature support. Keep a durable authority: An indexed copy can lag behind its source. Plan reindexing, retention, availability and recovery rather than assuming the search engine replaces every transactional database.

11.title: Ingestion, search and dashboards are separate components
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Ingest and transform: Supported Logstash or managed ingestion pipelines collect and transform events. Protect credentials, buffer failures and monitor rejected records. Index the documents: Mappings, shard design and lifecycle settings affect search behavior, scale and storage cost. Validate document shape before indexing at volume. Explore the results: OpenSearch Dashboards queries indexed data for visual analysis. It does not itself replace every log collector or define the source's retention policy.

11.title: A DynamoDB search index is an asynchronously maintained view
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Keep transactional operations on DynamoDB: Use the table's API for authoritative item reads and writes. Search uses a separate OpenSearch endpoint. Process changes into documents: The PDF's Streams-to-Lambda pattern can maintain the index. Handle retries, deletes, duplicate delivery and event ordering or document versioning. Build a repair path: Monitor lag and failed indexing. Backfill or reindex from a trusted source after gaps; current managed integration options also need their own compatibility checks.

11.title: Choose a CloudWatch Logs delivery path by latency and operations
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Use a supported subscription: A subscription filter can deliver matching log events through a supported Lambda-based OpenSearch integration. Permissions, retries and destination capacity matter. Buffer through Firehose: A supported Data Firehose path buffers delivery into OpenSearch. Buffer settings trade latency for throughput and request behavior. Verify both paths: Do not describe either route as zero-latency or loss-proof. Monitor delivery errors, rejected documents, retry limits and recovery storage.

11.title: DocumentDB compatibility requires application validation
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Use the document model: DocumentDB supports selected MongoDB-compatible APIs for JSON-like documents, queries and indexes. It is not the MongoDB engine itself. Understand the deployment: Supported instance-based clusters use a primary, replicas and distributed storage across three AZs. Other deployment types have different limits and behavior. Test real compatibility: Validate drivers, operators, indexes, transactions and failover with the actual application. A compatibility label is not proof that every MongoDB feature works.

11.title: DocumentDB cost depends on storage configuration and workload
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Account for compute and storage: Instance-based deployments charge for database instances and stored data. Benchmark representative reads/writes and verify current Region-specific pricing.

11.title: Time-series databases organize values around time and dimensions
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Model the observations: Use timestamps, dimensions and measures for IoT or operational metrics. Multi-measure records and time-aware queries can reduce repetitive application logic. Understand historical LiveAnalytics: Its design combines recent memory storage with historical magnetic storage, SQL, scheduled queries and time-series functions, with encryption in transit and at rest. Check current eligibility: Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers on 20 June 2025. Evaluate the current Timestream for InfluxDB options separately; do not assume identical APIs or tiering.

11.title: A time-series pipeline needs validated producers and consumers
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Ingest supported records: IoT applications, Kinesis, Lambda or supported stream-processing components can transform events into the selected time-series service's write format. Control event time: Handle late arrivals, retries, duplicates and retention. Producer throughput does not prove successful persistence or query readiness. Expose useful analysis: Use supported SQL/JDBC, dashboard or machine-learning integrations for the chosen product. The PDF's LiveAnalytics integrations do not automatically apply to InfluxDB.

11.title: DynamoDB walkthrough: prove a key query and index query
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Create an illustrative table: In a sandbox, create a table with PK and SK. Write USER#42/GAME#101 and USER#42/GAME#102 items with different result values. Verify the access path: Query PK=USER#42 and a supported SK condition. Compare it with a Scan and inspect consumed capacity and pagination behavior. Test an alternate key: Create an appropriate GSI for the alternate access pattern, wait for it to become active and query it. Expect eventual consistency and clean up sandbox resources.

11.title: RDS recovery walkthrough: restore before changing production DNS
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Inspect the recovery point: In a sandbox, confirm a usable snapshot or latest restorable time, the engine/version and the required KMS key permissions. Restore and validate: Create a new private database with the intended subnet/security settings. Connect using authorized credentials and verify representative records and application operations. Rehearse cutover: Update only the sandbox application's endpoint, reconnect and measure recovery time. Retain a clear rollback decision and remove test resources afterwards.

11.title: Proxy walkthrough: test pooling under a controlled burst
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Prepare the sandbox path: Create a supported proxy for the intended database. Configure private reachability, security groups and the selected authentication method. Compare connection behavior: Send a bounded test workload through the proxy and compare client connections with database connections. Inspect borrow latency, capacity and session pinning. Validate failure and cleanup: Test a denied principal or blocked path deliberately, then restore the configuration. Close clients and remove temporary resources after collecting the evidence.

11.title: Cache walkthrough: demonstrate a hit, stale value and refresh
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Observe the first read: Use a sandbox application with a database and cache. Start with a missing cache key; confirm the source read and cache fill. Make freshness visible: Read again to demonstrate a hit, then change the source value. Observe the selected invalidation or TTL behavior rather than claiming instant refresh. Verify recovery: Remove or expire the cache value and prove the application returns the correct source result. Test a controlled cache outage, then clean up the sandbox.

11.title: Aurora imports and exports S3 data through engine-specific features
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Choose the engine operation: Supported Aurora MySQL configurations use LOAD DATA FROM S3 and SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3. Aurora PostgreSQL uses supported aws_s3 extension functions instead. Prepare both permission layers: Grant the cluster the required S3 and applicable KMS permissions and network path. The database user also needs the engine-specific SQL privilege or role. Validate the data movement: Check format, engine/version, Region and account restrictions. A data export is not a complete transactional database backup; verify the intended import or query result.

11.title: RDS event notifications complement metrics and query evidence
11.imageBrief: Module 09 style. Subscribe to useful events: An RDS event subscription selects supported resources and categories such as backup, failover or configuration changes, using an SNS topic for notifications. Prepare reliable consumers: Confirm required subscriptions and permissions. Notifications can be delayed and are not guaranteed to arrive in event order; design automation around verified resource state. Correlate the symptom: An operational event is different from CPU metrics, database waits and SQL audit records. Combine the signals that answer the question before taking a recovery action.

12.title: A container packages an application, not an entire machine
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Package dependencies: An image bundles application code and required user-space dependencies. A running container is an instance of that image; keep durable state outside its replaceable writable layer. Match the runtime: CPU architecture, operating-system family and kernel compatibility still matter. A Linux image does not run natively on every Windows host simply because it is a container. Control resources: Set suitable CPU and memory reservations or limits. Shared-kernel efficiency can improve density, but startup time and isolation depend on the workload and runtime. Diagram: Image→two compatible Linux containers on shared kernel; separate incompatible Windows host crossed. No universal any-OS claim.

12.title: Choose orchestration separately from container compute
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Select an API: ECS uses AWS-native task and service concepts. EKS exposes managed Kubernetes APIs and its ecosystem. Existing Kubernetes practices can favor EKS, with operational trade-offs. Select compute: EC2 gives instance-level control and capacity responsibility. Fargate runs supported ECS tasks or EKS Pods without customer-managed worker instances. Keep ownership clear: Serverless compute does not remove image maintenance, permissions, networking, application health or cost control. Match platform constraints before migrating. Diagram: Matrix ECS/EKS rows EC2/Fargate columns, four compatible deployment choices, ownership symbols.

12.title: ECS turns task definitions into running work
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Define the workload: A versioned task definition describes one or more containers, their image, resources, ports and runtime settings. A task is a running instantiation of that definition. Maintain a service: A service maintains desired task count and replaces failed tasks according to its configuration. A standalone task can run finite work without a continuously maintained service. Group the capacity: A cluster is a logical grouping for tasks, services and capacity. It is not restricted to a collection of EC2 machines; eligible Fargate workloads also belong to clusters. Diagram: Task definition revision→service desired2→two tasks inside logical ECS cluster, one finite task beside service.

Maintain a service: A service maintains desired task count and replaces failed tasks according to its configuration. A standalone task can run finite work without a continuously maintained service.
Group the capacity: A cluster is a logical grouping for tasks, services and capacity. It is not restricted to a collection of EC2 machines; eligible Fargate workloads also belong to clusters.

12.title: A task definition makes deployment requirements explicit
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Pin a reproducible image: Choose the image reference and compatible platform. A digest identifies immutable content more precisely than a movable tag; ensure the application listens on the declared container port. Budget the task: Specify supported task CPU and memory combinations, container resource settings and essential containers. Add log configuration, environment references and required storage deliberately. Version and replace: Register a new revision for changed settings, then update the service or run a new task. An old running task does not automatically become the new definition. Diagram: Revision7 image digest+CPU+memory+port+logs→new tasks; old revision6 tasks retained until controlled replacement.

12.title: ECS application permissions differ from startup permissions
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Use a task role: Application SDK calls use the task IAM role, such as permission for one S3 prefix or DynamoDB table. Avoid static keys inside the image. Use an execution role: The ECS or Fargate agent uses the execution role for supported image pulls, log delivery and secret retrieval. Grant startup permissions separately from application data access. Protect host credentials: EC2 container instances have their own instance profile. Restrict metadata access and host privileges; shared-host containers do not become a hard tenant boundary merely because roles differ. Diagram: Three independent lanes App→S3 taskrole; Agent→ECR/logs executionrole; EC2host→ECS instanceprofile.

12.title: Load-balancer targets must match the task network mode
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Map bridge ports: On eligible EC2 bridge-mode tasks, a dynamic host port lets multiple copies of one container port share a host. ECS registers the instance and selected host port with the target group. Target task addresses: For awsvpc tasks, including Fargate, use IP target groups for the task ENI addresses. ALB HTTP routing and NLB connection behavior serve different ingress needs. Validate availability: Allow the correct load-balancer-to-target security path and health-check port. Multiple tasks on one host do not protect against that host failing; spread tasks across failure domains. Diagram: Left ALB→EC2:32768/container8080 and EC2:32769/container8080. Right ALB→taskENI10.0.1.10:8080 and taskENI10.0.2.10:8080 acrossAZs.

12.title: ECS network modes change address and isolation boundaries
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Compare Linux EC2 modes: Bridge uses a container network with host port mappings. Host shares the instance network and its port constraints. None provides no external connectivity or port mappings. Use awsvpc deliberately: Each task receives an ENI and private address, with task-level security groups and Flow Logs visibility. Fargate requires this mode rather than merely defaulting to it. Check platform limits: Windows and external-instance mode support differs from Linux EC2. Account for subnet addresses, ENI capacity and security controls before assuming another task can start. Diagram: Four labeled mini-modes none/bridge/host/awsvpc with ENI boundary and task security group.

12.title: A private Fargate task still needs startup connectivity
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Reach required services: A task must retrieve its image, obtain required secrets and send configured logs. Private placement alone does not create these service paths. Choose the egress path: Use suitable NAT connectivity or supported VPC endpoints. Private ECR pulls commonly need ECR API and registry endpoints plus S3 access for image layers; logs and secrets need their own paths. Separate network from IAM: Check subnet routes, endpoint policies, security-group rules and execution-role permissions. An image-pull error can be a network or authorization problem. Diagram: Private task→ECR API/registry interface endpoints; separate task→S3 gateway endpoint image layers; task→logs/secrets endpoints. No publicIP assumed.

12.title: Inject secrets without freezing credentials into images
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Reference protected values: Use supported Secrets Manager or Parameter Store references in task configuration. The execution role needs retrieval permission and applicable KMS access. Understand refresh timing: Environment-variable injection occurs when a task starts. Rotating the stored secret does not rewrite an existing process environment; deploy replacement tasks or use an application retrieval strategy. Limit exposure: Avoid printing values in logs or embedding them in image layers. Secure diagnostic access and define how a failed rotation or rollout recovers. Diagram: Secretv1→taskstart envv1; secretrotatesv2→newtask envv2; oldtask staysv1 untilreplaced.

12.title: Choose a service for continuous work and tasks for finite work
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Serve microservices: An ECS service can maintain replicas behind supported ALB or NLB integrations, with service discovery and configured scaling. Externalize shared state so tasks remain replaceable. Schedule finite jobs: Run standalone tasks for batch-style work or invoke tasks through a supported scheduler. Define retries, idempotency and completion evidence; a schedule does not prove success. Migrate deliberately: Containerize a legacy application, validate dependencies and storage, then test on compatible compute. On-Demand, Spot and eligible commitment discounts describe capacity or billing, not a special Reserved launch type. Migrate deliberately: Containerize a legacy application, validate dependencies and storage, then test on compatible compute. On-Demand, Spot and eligible commitment discounts describe capacity or billing, not a special Reserved launch type.

12.title: ECS service scaling changes tasks, not the EC2 fleet
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Track useful demand: Application Auto Scaling adjusts desired task count within configured bounds. Constrain traffic and identity: Use an enforcing network-policy implementation, required DNS allowances, least-privilege workload IAM and restricted metadata access. Default-deny intent needs an actual policy engine.

Choose stronger separation: Shared nodes share a kernel and other resources. For untrusted tenants, evaluate dedicated nodes, clusters or accounts and test both data access and resource-exhaustion boundaries.
12.decisionCue: Test the boundary with negative access attempts.

12.title: ECS walkthrough: prove rollout health before retiring old tasks
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Prepare a sandbox service: Use a trusted test image and explicit container port, execution role, subnets and security groups. Select a supported target group and a useful health endpoint. Deploy and inspect: Create a service with two replicas across suitable AZs. Inspect service events, running tasks and target health; send a test request and confirm the expected release response. Change and verify: Deploy a new task-definition revision and observe replacement health. Deliberately test a failing health endpoint in the sandbox, recover or roll back, collect evidence and remove temporary resources. Diagram: IllustrativeconsoleECS desired2/running2,ALB2healthy,revisionv2→healthverify→retirev1. No claimactualAWSexecution.
learningNotes: Prepare a sandbox service: Use a trusted test image and explicit container port, execution role, subnets and security groups. Select a supported target group and a useful health endpoint.
Deploy and inspect: Create a service with two replicas across suitable AZs. Inspect service events, running tasks and target health; send a test request and confirm the expected release response.

Change and verify: Deploy a new task-definition revision and observe replacement health. Deliberately test a failing health endpoint in the sandbox, recover or roll back, collect evidence and remove temporary resources.
12.decisionCue: A running task count is not proof of a healthy rollout.

12.title: ECR walkthrough: verify digest, findings and retention before release
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Push a sandbox release: Create an authorized private repository, authenticate with a short-lived registry credential and push a trusted test image. Record the resulting digest and intended tag. Inspect the controls: Inspect supported scan findings, repository access and tag settings. Preview a lifecycle policy and verify that the known-good rollback digest remains outside the deletion set. Verify distribution: If testing replication, push a new image after rules are active and verify its destination digest. Remove test images or repositories only after collecting evidence and considering dependent deployments. Diagram: IllustrativeECRdigestsha256… source/destinationmatch;scanfindingsreview;lifecyclepreviewrollbackretained.
learningNotes: Push a sandbox release: Create an authorized private repository, authenticate with a short-lived registry credential and push a trusted test image. Record the resulting digest and intended tag.
Inspect the controls: Inspect supported scan findings, repository access and tag settings. Preview a lifecycle policy and verify that the known-good rollback digest remains outside the deletion set.

Verify distribution: If testing replication, push a new image after rules are active and verify its destination digest. Remove test images or repositories only after collecting evidence and considering dependent deployments.
12.decisionCue: Release identity is the digest, not the appearance of a tag.

12.title: EKS walkthrough: follow a Pending Pod to its scheduling constraint
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Deploy bounded test work: Use a sandbox namespace, trusted image, resource requests and a non-production service account. Apply a small deployment and inspect Pod and node status. Read the evidence: Use kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod and suitable logs to distinguish scheduling, image-pull, readiness and runtime failures. Match events to the actual layer before changing settings. Validate the correction: Correct the specific resource, node-selector or storage-topology constraint in the sandbox. Observe Ready replicas and a successful request, then remove test resources and confirm no persistent storage is unintentionally left behind. Diagram: Illustrativekubectl PodPending eventInsufficientcpu→adjustboundedrequest/eligiblecapacity→Ready2/2; no fabricatedrealexecution.
learningNotes: Deploy bounded test work: Use a sandbox namespace, trusted image, resource requests and a non-production service account. Apply a small deployment and inspect Pod and node status.

Read the evidence: Use kubectl get pods, kubectl describe pod and suitable logs to distinguish scheduling, image-pull, readiness and runtime failures. Match events to the actual layer before changing settings.

Validate the correction: Correct the specific resource, node-selector or storage-topology constraint in the sandbox. Observe Ready replicas and a successful request, then remove test resources and confirm no persistent storage is unintentionally left behind.
12.decisionCue: A Pending Pod needs event evidence before more nodes.

12.title: Isolation walkthrough: prove allowed traffic and denied tenant access
12.imageBrief: Module09 style. Define the expected matrix: In a sandbox, write down which tenant identities may call each service or data path. Include DNS and required platform dependencies before applying default-deny network policies. Exercise both outcomes: Run an authorized same-tenant request and a cross-tenant negative test. Check application authorization, workload IAM and supported network-policy logs or evidence independently. Record the boundary: Confirm the denied request cannot read another tenant’s records. Preserve policy versions and results, then remove test resources; one network timeout alone does not prove data isolation. Diagram: TenantA→AdataALLOW;TenantA→BdataDENY;network/IAM/appauth3gates;testmatrix.
learningNotes: Define the expected matrix: In a sandbox, write down which tenant identities may call each service or data path. Include DNS and required platform dependencies before applying default-deny network policies.

Exercise both outcomes: Run an authorized same-tenant request and a cross-tenant negative test. Check application authorization, workload IAM and supported network-policy logs or evidence independently.

Record the boundary: Confirm the denied request cannot read another tenant’s records. Preserve policy versions and results, then remove test resources; one network timeout alone does not prove data isolation.
12.decisionCue: A boundary is demonstrated by both allowed and denied behavior.

13.title: Lambda executes events in replaceable environments
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Start from an event: A trigger supplies an event to a handler. Lambda initializes a compatible runtime, invokes your code and may reuse the environment for later work. Externalize durable state: Keep authoritative data in a suitable database or object store. Reused memory and temporary files can improve efficiency, but they are not a durable session store. Separate responsibilities: AWS operates the managed platform. You own code, dependencies, permissions, input validation, idempotency and downstream capacity. Diagram: EventBridge -> Lambda execution environment containing Init and Invoke(handler). Independent handler branch -> external durable DynamoDB/S3. Separate dashed reuse loop back to handler, labelled possible/not guaranteed; no reuse router box.
learningNotes: Start from an event: A trigger supplies an event to a handler. Lambda initializes a compatible runtime, invokes your code and may reuse the environment for later work.
Externalize durable state: Keep authoritative data in a suitable database or object store. Reused memory and temporary files can improve efficiency, but they are not a durable session store.
Separate responsibilities: AWS operates the managed platform. You own code, dependencies, permissions, input validation, idempotency and downstream capacity.
13.decisionCue: Environment reuse is an optimization, not a state guarantee.

13.title: A Lambda image must follow the Lambda runtime contract
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Choose a supported runtime: Managed runtime families include Node.js, Python, Java, .NET and Ruby; supported versions change. Custom runtimes can use the Runtime API for languages such as Go or Rust. Package deliberately: ZIP deployments and compatible container images have different packaging paths. A container image still needs the Lambda Runtime API and compatible architecture/operating system. Use the right compute: ECS or Fargate can suit an arbitrary long-running container. A generic Docker image is not automatically a Lambda function; keep dependencies patched. Diagram: Compare ZIP + managed runtime and compatible ECR image + Runtime API feeding Lambda; arbitrary server container branches to ECS/Fargate.
learningNotes: Choose a supported runtime: Managed runtime families include Node.js, Python, Java, .NET and Ruby; supported versions change. Custom runtimes can use the Runtime API for languages such as Go or Rust.

Package deliberately: ZIP deployments and compatible container images have different packaging paths. A container image still needs the Lambda Runtime API and compatible architecture/operating system.
Use the right compute: ECS or Fargate can suit an arbitrary long-running container. A generic Docker image is not automatically a Lambda function; keep dependencies patched.
13.decisionCue: Container packaging does not remove the runtime contract.

13.title: Memory changes CPU allocation and execution economics
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Tune measured demand: For standard Event Functions, memory is configurable from 128 to 10,240 MB. CPU allocation increases with memory; 1,769 MB gives the equivalent of one vCPU, not two. Bound execution time: A standard invocation can run up to 900 seconds. Set a timeout that fits the caller and downstream system; a longer Lambda timeout does not extend an API integration automatically. Treat temporary storage separately: Configurable /tmp storage spans 512 to 10,240 MB. It is temporary environment storage; do not confuse it with function memory or a durable database. Diagram: Memory slider -> proportional CPU; separate /tmp disk slider; caller timeout and Lambda timeout shown as independent clocks. Visibly correct one-vCPU value.
learningNotes: Tune measured demand: For standard Event Functions, memory is configurable from 128 to 10,240 MB. CPU allocation increases with memory; 1,769 MB gives the equivalent of one vCPU, not two.

Bound execution time: A standard invocation can run up to 900 seconds. Set a timeout that fits the caller and downstream system; a longer Lambda timeout does not extend an API integration automatically.
Treat temporary storage separately: Configurable /tmp storage spans 512 to 10,240 MB. It is temporary environment storage; do not confuse it with function memory or a durable database.
13.decisionCue: Benchmark duration and cost together; more memory can finish sooner.

13.title: Check every package and payload boundary in the path
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Deploy within package limits: ZIP direct upload is limited to 50 MB compressed; uncompressed code plus layers is limited to 250 MB. A compatible container image can be up to 10 GB uncompressed. Distinguish invocation modes: Standard buffered synchronous requests and responses allow 6 MB each; asynchronous invocation payloads allow 1 MB. Streamed responses use a separate supported contract. Design for the smallest gate: A front door, event producer or destination may impose a smaller limit. Put large objects in S3 and pass a scoped reference when the full chain cannot carry the data. Diagram: API -> Lambda -> destination with different size gates; separate S3 large object and small reference; do not imply API 10 MB passes through 6 MB Lambda.
learningNotes: Deploy within package limits: ZIP direct upload is limited to 50 MB compressed; uncompressed code plus layers is limited to 250 MB. A compatible container image can be up to 10 GB uncompressed.
Distinguish invocation modes: Standard buffered synchronous requests and responses allow 6 MB each; asynchronous invocation payloads allow 1 MB. Streamed responses use a separate supported contract.
Design for the smallest gate: A front door, event producer or destination may impose a smaller limit. Put large objects in S3 and pass a scoped reference when the full chain cannot carry the data.
13.decisionCue: The smallest compatible limit controls the end-to-end design.

13.title: Concurrency protects both shared capacity and dependencies
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Estimate in-flight work: Concurrency is the number of simultaneous invocations. For a steady example, 200 requests per second times 0.5 seconds average duration requires about 100 concurrent executions. Isolate critical capacity: Reserved concurrency reserves a function share and caps its maximum. It can protect another function from a noisy neighbor and limit pressure on a database. Handle throttling: The usual regional account default is 1,000, with new-account reductions and approved increases possible. Observe throttles, retry with backoff where appropriate and respect scaling rates. Diagram: Shared pool split into reserved critical function and unreserved functions; noisy stream blocked at cap before database. Equation 200 x 0.5 = 100.
learningNotes: Estimate in-flight work: Concurrency is the number of simultaneous invocations. For a steady example, 200 requests per second times 0.5 seconds average duration requires about 100 concurrent executions.
Isolate critical capacity: Reserved concurrency reserves a function share and caps its maximum. It can protect another function from a noisy neighbor and limit pressure on a database.

Handle throttling: The usual regional account default is 1,000, with new-account reductions and approved increases possible. Observe throttles, retry with backoff where appropriate and respect scaling rates.
13.decisionCue: Reserved capacity is not a pre-initialized environment.

13.title: Reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency and SnapStart differ
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Reserve a share: Reserved concurrency controls capacity allocation and the function ceiling. It does not run initialization ahead of an invocation. Pre-initialize for latency: Provisioned concurrency maintains ready environments for a qualified version or alias and adds charges. Requests beyond it may use on-demand capacity if other limits allow. Restore supported snapshots: SnapStart reduces initialization for supported runtimes/configurations. Validate compatibility and restore-time uniqueness; it cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency. Diagram: Three labeled columns: reserved slots, ready environments, snapshot restore. Separate capacity versus latency labels; no combined SnapStart + provisioned configuration.
learningNotes: Reserve a share: Reserved concurrency controls capacity allocation and the function ceiling. It does not run initialization ahead of an invocation.

Pre-initialize for latency: Provisioned concurrency maintains ready environments for a qualified version or alias and adds charges. Requests beyond it may use on-demand capacity if other limits allow.

Restore supported snapshots: SnapStart reduces initialization for supported runtimes/configurations. Validate compatibility and restore-time uniqueness; it cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency.
13.decisionCue: Choose capacity isolation separately from startup-latency optimization.

13.title: A published version and an alias support safer traffic shifts
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Freeze a release: Publish an immutable function version after validating code and configuration. An alias provides a stable qualified name pointing to a selected release. Shift traffic deliberately: CodeDeploy can automate all-at-once, linear or canary shifts between versions. SAM can define the function, deployment preferences and required infrastructure. Watch and roll back: Use pre/post traffic hooks and CloudWatch alarms to validate health. A traffic shift is a deployment control, not proof that new code preserves data compatibility. Diagram: Alias -> v1 90% and v2 10%, CodeDeploy timeline then alarm branch rollback; label percentages sum100. SAM configuration separate from runtime request path.
learningNotes: Freeze a release: Publish an immutable function version after validating code and configuration. An alias provides a stable qualified name pointing to a selected release.
Shift traffic deliberately: CodeDeploy can automate all-at-once, linear or canary shifts between versions. SAM can define the function, deployment preferences and required infrastructure.
Watch and roll back: Use pre/post traffic hooks and CloudWatch alarms to validate health. A traffic shift is a deployment control, not proof that new code preserves data compatibility.
13.decisionCue: Use versioned releases, measured traffic shifts and a tested rollback.

13.title: Logs, metrics and traces explain different failure layers
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Capture execution evidence: The execution role needs supported CloudWatch Logs permissions. Correlate structured logs with request identifiers and protect secrets and personal data. Measure symptoms: Inspect invocations, errors, duration, throttles and concurrency. Add initialization and downstream latency evidence before changing memory or capacity. Trace with current tooling: Use supported Lambda/X-Ray tracing permissions and instrumentation. X-Ray SDKs/daemon entered maintenance in February 2026; prefer current OpenTelemetry instrumentation guidance. Diagram: Lambda connected to three distinct evidence panels: Logs(request id), Metrics(duration/errors), Trace(downstream segments). Current OpenTelemetry -> X-Ray, not false service retirement.
learningNotes: Capture execution evidence: The execution role needs supported CloudWatch Logs permissions. Correlate structured logs with request identifiers and protect secrets and personal data.
Measure symptoms: Inspect invocations, errors, duration, throttles and concurrency. Add initialization and downstream latency evidence before changing memory or capacity.

Trace with current tooling: Use supported Lambda/X-Ray tracing permissions and instrumentation. X-Ray SDKs/daemon entered maintenance in February 2026; prefer current OpenTelemetry instrumentation guidance.
13.decisionCue: A trace, a log and a metric answer different questions.

13.title: VPC attachment supplies a private path, not automatic internet
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Attach for private resources: Configure suitable VPC subnets and security groups for private RDS or other dependencies. Lambda uses service-managed networking and Hyperplane ENIs for this access. Check every network gate: Validate ENI permissions, DNS, subnet addresses, routes and security groups. Database authorization remains separate from network reachability. Plan public access: A public subnet does not give a Lambda function a public IP. Private IPv4 egress usually needs a working NAT path; supported AWS endpoints can avoid internet paths for those services. Diagram: Lambda service -> Hyperplane ENI in private subnet -> private RDS via SG; separate route toward NAT/public endpoint. Explicit public-subnet-alone != internet badge.
learningNotes: Attach for private resources: Configure suitable VPC subnets and security groups for private RDS or other dependencies. Lambda uses service-managed networking and Hyperplane ENIs for this access.
Check every network gate: Validate ENI permissions, DNS, subnet addresses, routes and security groups. Database authorization remains separate from network reachability.

Plan public access: A public subnet does not give a Lambda function a public IP. Private IPv4 egress usually needs a working NAT path; supported AWS endpoints can avoid internet paths for those services.
13.decisionCue: VPC connectivity, internet egress and data permissions are separate.

13.title: A NAT egress path can provide a stable public IPv4 identity
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Route from private subnets: Send required IPv4 internet traffic from the function network path to a public NAT gateway in a suitable public subnet. Complete the path: The NAT gateway uses an Elastic IP and an internet-gateway route. External systems see the NAT egress identity; Lambda itself still has no public IPv4 address. Design availability and cost: Use deliberate AZ routing and allowlist all possible egress addresses. Include NAT processing, transfer, routing and dependency failure in the design. Diagram: Private subnet Lambda/ENI -> public subnet NAT(EIP) -> IGW -> external allowlist API; arrows routed correctly distinct subnet boundaries; show EIP on NAT only.
learningNotes: Route from private subnets: Send required IPv4 internet traffic from the function network path to a public NAT gateway in a suitable public subnet.
Complete the path: The NAT gateway uses an Elastic IP and an internet-gateway route. External systems see the NAT egress identity; Lambda itself still has no public IPv4 address.
Design availability and cost: Use deliberate AZ routing and allowlist all possible egress addresses. Include NAT processing, transfer, routing and dependency failure in the design.
13.decisionCue: A fixed egress IP belongs to the NAT path, not the function.

13.title: Synchronous invocation leaves retry decisions with the caller
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Wait for the outcome: A direct SDK/CLI request or API integration waits for a result within its own timeout and response contract. Interpret both layers: A successful transport response does not always mean function success. Check function error indicators or the front-door status and correlated logs. Retry deliberately: Use bounded backoff, jitter and idempotency for retryable failures. Retrying a completed write after a lost response can create duplicate side effects. Diagram: Caller -> Lambda with response arrow returning outcome; lost-response scenario after committed DBwrite -> retry -> idempotency record prevents duplicate.
learningNotes: Wait for the outcome: A direct SDK/CLI request or API integration waits for a result within its own timeout and response contract.
Interpret both layers: A successful transport response does not always mean function success. Check function error indicators or the front-door status and correlated logs.
Retry deliberately: Use bounded backoff, jitter and idempotency for retryable failures. Retrying a completed write after a lost response can create duplicate side effects.
13.decisionCue: A timeout can leave the business outcome uncertain.

13.title: Asynchronous acceptance is not successful processing
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Queue before execution: Supported sources such as S3, SNS and EventBridge can invoke Lambda asynchronously. Acceptance places an event in Lambda-managed processing; it is not a final application result. Separate retry classes: By default, function errors get two additional attempts. Throttling and system errors follow queue retry behavior for up to six hours by default, subject to configuration and age. Expect duplicates: An event can be delivered more than once, even without a function error. Use stable event identifiers, safe writes and monitored failure retention. Diagram: Source -> async queue(accepted) -> function attempt1,error -> retry2 -> retry3 -> failure retention; side note throttles/system errors have different age/retry path.
learningNotes: Queue before execution: Supported sources such as S3, SNS and EventBridge can invoke Lambda asynchronously. Acceptance places an event in Lambda-managed processing; it is not a final application result.

Separate retry classes: By default, function errors get two additional attempts. Throttling and system errors follow queue retry behavior for up to six hours by default, subject to configuration and age.
Expect duplicates: An event can be delivered more than once, even without a function error. Use stable event identifiers, safe writes and monitored failure retention.
13.decisionCue: Three attempts describes default function errors, not every failure.

13.title: Destinations retain an outcome; a DLQ retains an event
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Choose retained evidence: An asynchronous destination includes an invocation record with request/response context. Configure success and failure destinations independently. Know destination support: Supported choices include standard SQS, standard SNS, Lambda and EventBridge; S3 is supported for failure records. A function DLQ uses standard SQS or SNS event content. Test delivery itself: The execution role needs destination permissions. Check size compatibility, encryption and DestinationDeliveryFailures; a failure archive is useless if delivery is denied. Diagram: Lambda outcome branches success destination record and failure destination record; separate DLQ originalevent panel. Annotate S3 failure-only and SNS256KB smaller-than-async.
learningNotes: Choose retained evidence: An asynchronous destination includes an invocation record with request/response context. Configure success and failure destinations independently.
Know destination support: Supported choices include standard SQS, standard SNS, Lambda and EventBridge; S3 is supported for failure records. A function DLQ uses standard SQS or SNS event content.
Test delivery itself: The execution role needs destination permissions. Check size compatibility, encryption and DestinationDeliveryFailures; a failure archive is useless if delivery is denied.
13.decisionCue: Successful function handling and successful failure-record delivery are separate checks.

13.title: A poll-based event source mapping has its own retry contract
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Let the mapping poll: Lambda event source mappings poll supported queues or streams such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams. They batch records and invoke the handler; this is not the async invocation queue. Control failed records: For SQS, align visibility, batch processing and supported partial-batch responses. For streams, checkpoints, ordering and retry/age settings affect backlog and poisoned records. Protect throughput: Tune source capacity, batch windows, concurrency and idempotency together. A queue buffers demand; it does not create infinite processing capacity. Diagram: SQS -> ESM poller -> Lambda handler; handler outcomes -> poller; poller deletes successful messages while failed messages remain until visibility/retry. Kinesis -> ESM checkpoint reader -> Lambda; failure retains checkpoint and retries existing records, never reinserts them.
learningNotes: Let the mapping poll: Lambda event source mappings poll supported queues or streams such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams. They batch records and invoke the handler; this is not the async invocation queue.

Control failed records: For SQS, align visibility, batch processing and supported partial-batch responses. For streams, checkpoints, ordering and retry/age settings affect backlog and poisoned records.
Protect throughput: Tune source capacity, batch windows, concurrency and idempotency together. A queue buffers demand; it does not create infinite processing capacity.
13.decisionCue: Match retries to the source integration, not just to Lambda.

13.title: A thumbnail workflow needs recursion and duplicate protection
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Separate input and output: Use a dedicated input prefix or bucket and a distinct thumbnail destination. Filter notifications so generated thumbnails do not trigger an endless loop. Process a stable object: Read the referenced object with scoped permissions, generate the image and write output plus useful metadata such as source identity, size and creation time. Handle partial completion: Object output and DynamoDB metadata writes are separate operations. Use deterministic keys, conditional/idempotent updates, retries and reconciliation for partial failures. Diagram: Original branching workflow inputphotos/ -> event -> Lambda -> thumbnails/ plus DynamoDBmetadata. No output-to-trigger loop; dedup key and partialfailure checkpointlabels.
learningNotes: Separate input and output: Use a dedicated input prefix or bucket and a distinct thumbnail destination. Filter notifications so generated thumbnails do not trigger an endless loop.
Process a stable object: Read the referenced object with scoped permissions, generate the image and write output plus useful metadata such as source identity, size and creation time.
Handle partial completion: Object output and DynamoDB metadata writes are separate operations. Use deterministic keys, conditional/idempotent updates, retries and reconciliation for partial failures.
13.decisionCue: An event-driven diagram still needs a consistency and recovery design.

13.title: Scheduled invocation requires permissions and execution evidence
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Choose a schedule: Use a supported EventBridge Scheduler configuration for hourly, cron or one-time work. Specify the intended timezone and flexible window behavior where relevant. Authorize the target: The scheduler execution role needs permission to invoke the qualified function. Configure supported retry and failed-delivery retention settings. Validate completion: Scheduler delivery success and handler business success are different signals. Make the job idempotent and monitor function results as well as target invocation failures. Diagram: Clock schedule -> Scheduler(executionrole) -> Lambda -> completedbusinessrecord; deliveryfailure branch vs processingfailure branch clearly separated.
learningNotes: Choose a schedule: Use a supported EventBridge Scheduler configuration for hourly, cron or one-time work. Specify the intended timezone and flexible window behavior where relevant.
Authorize the target: The scheduler execution role needs permission to invoke the qualified function. Configure supported retry and failed-delivery retention settings.
Validate completion: Scheduler delivery success and handler business success are different signals. Make the job idempotent and monitor function results as well as target invocation failures.
13.decisionCue: A schedule firing does not prove that the job finished.

13.title: Fan-out and buffering trade latency for controlled work intake
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Fan out notifications: An S3 event can reach SNS and independently subscribed consumers. Each subscription needs its own delivery/security design. Insert a queue intentionally: SNS to SQS to a Lambda poller provides buffering, batching and separate consumer pacing. It adds queueing delay and new retention/retry responsibilities. Keep payload semantics clear: Raw-message delivery versus an SNS envelope changes the handler input. Handle duplicates and recover the correct business event rather than assuming identical payloads. Diagram: Original comparison: SNS branches two independent consumers; lower lane SNS->SQS backlog->poller->Lambda, annotate paced batches and added latency.
learningNotes: Fan out notifications: An S3 event can reach SNS and independently subscribed consumers. Each subscription needs its own delivery/security design.
Insert a queue intentionally: SNS to SQS to a Lambda poller provides buffering, batching and separate consumer pacing. It adds queueing delay and new retention/retry responsibilities.
Keep payload semantics clear: Raw-message delivery versus an SNS envelope changes the handler input. Handle duplicates and recover the correct business event rather than assuming identical payloads.
13.decisionCue: A buffer absorbs bursts only within its retention and processing limits.

13.title: Current Lambda offerings have different execution contracts
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Keep the standard scope: The course core uses standard event-driven Lambda functions. Its ordinary per-invocation duration, memory and concurrency limits must be labelled with that scope. Recognize supported exceptions: Lambda Managed Instances uses supported EC2 capacity with Lambda-managed operations. Eligible asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations can run up to 90 minutes, with source exceptions. Separate durable orchestration: Durable functions checkpoint and resume supported multi-step code; wall-clock workflow duration is not one uninterrupted invocation. Newer Lambda offerings require their own current compatibility and quota check. Diagram: Three separate cards: standard event function 15-min invocation; ManagedInstances eligible90-min; durable checkpoints+wait+resume. Label supplementary current-AWS context.
learningNotes: Keep the standard scope: The course core uses standard event-driven Lambda functions. Its ordinary per-invocation duration, memory and concurrency limits must be labelled with that scope.

Recognize supported exceptions: Lambda Managed Instances uses supported EC2 capacity with Lambda-managed operations. Eligible asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations can run up to 90 minutes, with source exceptions.

Separate durable orchestration: Durable functions checkpoint and resume supported multi-step code; wall-clock workflow duration is not one uninterrupted invocation. Newer Lambda offerings require their own current compatibility and quota check.
13.decisionCue: Do not turn a standard-function limit into a universal Lambda claim.

13.title: Invocation permission differs from the function execution role
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Authorize the caller: The invoking principal or service must be allowed to invoke the selected function/version/alias. Scope service resource policies to the expected source where supported. Authorize the code: The execution role authorizes what handler code can do, including selected database, object, secret, logging and destination operations. Protect credentials and inputs: Use temporary credentials, scoped secret retrieval and supported encryption. Validate events and avoid leaking tokens or secret values into logs and error responses. Diagram: Caller/service -> invocation permission gate -> Lambda; separate execution-role gate -> S3/DynamoDB/Secrets. Never draw callerpolicy as automatically grantingfunctiondataaccess.
learningNotes: Authorize the caller: The invoking principal or service must be allowed to invoke the selected function/version/alias. Scope service resource policies to the expected source where supported.
Authorize the code: The execution role authorizes what handler code can do, including selected database, object, secret, logging and destination operations.
Protect credentials and inputs: Use temporary credentials, scoped secret retrieval and supported encryption. Validate events and avoid leaking tokens or secret values into logs and error responses.
13.decisionCue: The caller invokes; the execution role accesses dependencies.

13.title: Choose REST, HTTP or WebSocket APIs by required features
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. REST API feature depth: Use REST API when supported requirements include usage plans/API keys, request validation, stage caching, WAF, private API endpoints or canary releases. HTTP API simplicity: HTTP APIs provide a leaner RESTful front door with supported JWT/IAM/Lambda authorization and integrations. They do not inherit every REST API feature. WebSocket interaction: WebSocket APIs keep client connections for bidirectional messages. Connection lifecycle, routes and backend callback permissions become part of the application. Diagram: Three product cards REST/HTTP/WebSocket with precisefeaturebadges and websocketsbidirectionalarrows. No RESTfeaturebadges underHTTP.
learningNotes: REST API feature depth: Use REST API when supported requirements include usage plans/API keys, request validation, stage caching, WAF, private API endpoints or canary releases.
HTTP API simplicity: HTTP APIs provide a leaner RESTful front door with supported JWT/IAM/Lambda authorization and integrations. They do not inherit every REST API feature.
WebSocket interaction: WebSocket APIs keep client connections for bidirectional messages. Connection lifecycle, routes and backend callback permissions become part of the application.
13.decisionCue: RESTful HTTP traffic does not identify the API Gateway product.

13.title: An integration connects API requests to a compatible backend
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Select the backend contract: API Gateway can integrate with Lambda, supported AWS service operations or HTTP endpoints. Select proxy versus custom mapping behavior intentionally. Transform and validate: Request parameters, body formats, status responses and error mappings depend on API/integration type. Importing OpenAPI helps define the contract but does not authorize the backend. Authorize and connect: Use supported invocation permissions or integration credentials, plus network reachability for private/on-premises dependencies. Do not expose arbitrary AWS APIs without a defined allowlist. Diagram: APImethod branches Lambda proxy, selectedAWSoperation, HTTPbackend; separate mapping/permission/networkgates, include onprem with validatedreachability.
learningNotes: Select the backend contract: API Gateway can integrate with Lambda, supported AWS service operations or HTTP endpoints. Select proxy versus custom mapping behavior intentionally.

Transform and validate: Request parameters, body formats, status responses and error mappings depend on API/integration type. Importing OpenAPI helps define the contract but does not authorize the backend.

Authorize and connect: Use supported invocation permissions or integration credentials, plus network reachability for private/on-premises dependencies. Do not expose arbitrary AWS APIs without a defined allowlist.
13.decisionCue: An integration is a contract, permission path and network path.

13.title: Direct AWS integration can remove an unnecessary function hop
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Map one supported operation: For simple authenticated intake, a supported API integration can call an operation such as sending a message to SQS or starting a workflow. Scope the integration role: Grant the minimum target action and resource. Validate input, translate the request shape and return a suitable acceptance response. Preserve business logic where needed: Removing a pass-through function can reduce code and an invocation hop. Keep compute when custom validation, orchestration or transformation actually requires it. Diagram: Compare client->API->pass-throughLambda->SQS with client->API(integrationrole scoped SendMessage)->SQS. Label enqueueacceptance!=jobcomplete.

13.decisionCue: Less code is useful only when the integration still meets the contract.

13.title: An API deployment stage and a Lambda alias are separate controls
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Deploy an API configuration: A REST API deployment captures API configuration; a named stage points to a deployment. Stage count is quota-bound, not literally unlimited. Route to a function release: The integration can invoke a qualified Lambda alias. API stage selection and alias version weighting are separate mechanisms with independent configuration. Change and recover deliberately: Use supported REST canary settings or controlled deployment changes; test permissions, stage variables, cached responses and client compatibility before rollback. Diagram: Two independentselectors APIstage->deployment and Lambdaprodalias->v1/v2; distinct knobs, no conflatingAPIcanarywithaliasweight.

13.decisionCue: API rollout and function rollout must be coordinated.

13.title: Time and payload limits depend on API type and transfer mode
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Check buffered constraints: A standard REST API payload limit is 10 MB. Buffered Lambda integration has its own 6-MB request/response boundary and format overhead. Qualify timeout claims: Regional and private REST integration timeouts can be raised beyond the usual 29 seconds, potentially reducing account throttle quota. HTTP and edge-optimized APIs have different limits. Recognize response streaming: Supported REST proxy response streaming can run up to 15 minutes and exceed buffered response sizes. It does not turn large uploads into streamed requests or remove downstream limits. Diagram: Three independentgates clientpayload, APIintegrationtimeout, Lambdabuffer; separate supportedRESTresponse-streaminglane(outboundonly).

13.title: Upload large objects directly with a tightly scoped S3 URL
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Authorize the upload request: The application asks a trusted API for upload permission. Validate user/tenant context, intended object key, expiry and allowed operation. Return a limited capability: A permitted signer creates a short-lived presigned request. The browser sends object bytes directly to S3 using the signed method and required headers. Validate the stored result: Configure S3 CORS where needed, encryption, size/checksum constraints and completion processing. A presigned URL is a bearer capability; protect it from disclosure. Diagram: Numbered arrows 1browser->API permission 2API->signer 3URLreturnbrowser 4browser->S3 directly. No largeupload throughLambda/API.

Validate the stored result: Configure S3 CORS where needed, encryption, size/checksum constraints and completion processing. A presigned URL is a bearer capability; protect it from disclosure.

13.title: Edge, Regional and private endpoints change the client path
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Edge-optimized REST: A managed CloudFront edge path fronts one regional API. Edge presence does not create independent multi-Region backends. Regional endpoint: Clients connect to a regional API endpoint; an intentionally configured CloudFront distribution can add edge behavior with explicit cache and origin settings. Private REST endpoint: Private API access uses execute-api interface endpoints and compatible private connectivity, endpoint/resource policies and API authorization. Diagram: Three separate paths: managed CloudFront->regional REST, direct regional REST with optional ownCloudFront, private client->execute-api interface endpoint->service-managed private REST API. Customer VPC contains client/endpoint only; API service outside.

Private REST endpoint: Private API access uses execute-api interface endpoints and compatible private connectivity, endpoint/resource policies and API authorization.
13.decisionCue: Endpoint location and backend resilience are separate decisions.

13.title: A private API combines network reachability and policy gates
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Create a private client path: Reach an execute-api interface endpoint through a VPC or supported connected network. Configure private DNS, subnet placement and endpoint security groups deliberately. Evaluate distinct policies: An endpoint policy and API resource policy restrict access; supported conditions include aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce. Method authorization still applies. Support intentional sharing: One endpoint can reach multiple permitted private APIs, including supported cross-account designs. Private connectivity does not make every API in the Region available. Diagram: Privateclient -> endpointSG -> endpointpolicy -> APIresourcepolicy -> methodauth -> API. CrossaccountAPI sidecard samegates; endpointsharedmultipleallowedAPIs.

Support intentional sharing: One endpoint can reach multiple permitted private APIs, including supported cross-account designs. Private connectivity does not make every API in the Region available.
13.decisionCue: Reachability is necessary; endpoint, resource and method authorization still matter.

13.title: Private backend integration is different from a private API
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Separate the two directions: A public API can reach a private backend through a VPC link. A private API controls how clients reach API Gateway; the two decisions are independent. Use current VPC-link support: Current REST VPC links V2 support compatible ALB/NLB private integrations. Legacy V1 uses its own narrower contract. HTTP APIs have separate integration options. Validate backend routing: Check ownership, listener ports, security groups, TLS server name and path mapping. REST private integrations can include the stage in the backend path unless overridden. Diagram: Internetclient->publicAPI->VPCLinkV2->privateALB->service; separate privateclient->privateAPI inset. ClearlyALBbehindVPCLink notpublicAPIitself.

Use current VPC-link support: Current REST VPC links V2 support compatible ALB/NLB private integrations. Legacy V1 uses its own narrower contract. HTTP APIs have separate integration options.
Validate backend routing: Check ownership, listener ports, security groups, TLS server name and path mapping. REST private integrations can include the stage in the backend path unless overridden.
13.decisionCue: Private ingress and private backend connectivity are different features.

13.title: A cache key is part of the authorization design
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Cache compatible responses: REST API stage caching reduces backend calls. Default TTL is 300 seconds, supported up to 3,600; TTL zero disables caching. GET caching is enabled by default when stage method caching is turned on. Separate users and variants: Select cache-key parameters that represent the actual response. Never serve one tenant’s private data to another through a shared cache key. Operate the cache: Method overrides, encryption, authorized invalidation and stage flush are separate controls. Monitor hits/misses, response size, stale data and hourly cache cost. Diagram: Cachelookup key(tenant+resource+variant) -> hitresponse or missbackend; two tenants separatedkeys; invalidationpermissiongate.

Separate users and variants: Select cache-key parameters that represent the actual response. Never serve one tenant’s private data to another through a shared cache key.
Operate the cache: Method overrides, encryption, authorized invalidation and stage flush are separate controls. Monitor hits/misses, response size, stale data and hourly cache cost.
13.decisionCue: Fast cached data is wrong if its identity or freshness boundary is wrong.

13.title: Authenticate callers with the mechanism the API supports
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. IAM and signed requests: AWS_IAM uses SigV4-signed requests with permitted identities. It suits authorized AWS callers; do not transmit a raw secret access key as a bearer token. Tokens and authorizers: REST supports Cognito user-pool and Lambda authorizers. HTTP APIs support compatible JWT authorizers, including suitable Cognito/OIDC issuers, plus supported IAM/Lambda options. Enforce application permissions: A valid identity is not blanket access to every record. Scope authorizer caching and check tenant/resource permissions in trusted application logic. Diagram: IAM caller signs API request. User/client signs in with Cognito or compatible issuer, issuer returns token to client, client sends token to API. Then separate application tenant/resource authorization gate. Issuer never sends client API request.

Tokens and authorizers: REST supports Cognito user-pool and Lambda authorizers. HTTP APIs support compatible JWT authorizers, including suitable Cognito/OIDC issuers, plus supported IAM/Lambda options.
Enforce application permissions: A valid identity is not blanket access to every record. Scope authorizer caching and check tenant/resource permissions in trusted application logic.
13.decisionCue: Validate identity, then authorize the requested operation and data.

13.title: Resource policies, backend roles and TLS solve different gates
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Restrict API invocation: A supported REST resource policy can restrict principals and network context. Explicit denies and cross-account policy requirements must be evaluated with method authorization. Allow the integration: Backend invocation needs compatible Lambda resource permission or an integration role scoped to the required AWS action. This is separate from the API caller’s data permissions. Secure the endpoint: Use compatible ACM certificates and custom-domain mappings with appropriate DNS records. Regional/edge certificate rules differ; a DNS alias is not authorization. Diagram: Actual HTTPS path caller->API Gateway custom-domain TLS endpoint->integration->Lambda and response back. Route53 lookup and ACM certificate are dotted side/configuration associations. Resource/method checks inside API; backend permission is logical annotation.

Allow the integration: Backend invocation needs compatible Lambda resource permission or an integration role scoped to the required AWS action. This is separate from the API caller’s data permissions.
Secure the endpoint: Use compatible ACM certificates and custom-domain mappings with appropriate DNS records. Regional/edge certificate rules differ; a DNS alias is not authorization.
13.decisionCue: Caller policy, integration policy and transport protection are not interchangeable.

13.title: CORS is a browser response rule, not an API access boundary
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Recognize the browser check: A browser compares origins and may send an OPTIONS preflight for the intended method and headers. Non-browser clients are not secured by CORS. Return compatible headers: Configure allowed origins, methods and headers on preflight and relevant actual/error responses. Credentialed requests require an explicit compatible origin, not a wildcard. Keep real authorization: IAM/token checks, tenant authorization and CSRF protections where applicable remain necessary. A browser can hide a response even though the backend already processed the request. Diagram: Browser OPTIONS->APIpreflightthenactualrequest->responseCORSgate; separateCLIpathstillneedsauthnoCORSgate. Showbackendmayexecuteevenifbrowserblocksresponse.

Return compatible headers: Configure allowed origins, methods and headers on preflight and relevant actual/error responses. Credentialed requests require an explicit compatible origin, not a wildcard.

Keep real authorization: IAM/token checks, tenant authorization and CSRF protections where applicable remain necessary. A browser can hide a response even though the backend already processed the request.

13.title: Usage-plan keys meter clients; they do not authenticate users
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Identify an API consumer: REST API keys can identify developer customers across associated stages and methods. A usage plan sets supported request-rate and period quota targets. Retain real authorization: Use IAM, a Cognito user pool or a compatible authorizer to protect access. A leaked API key is not a trustworthy user or tenant identity. Budget for best effort: Usage-plan quotas and throttling are best effort, not hard spending caps. Regional/account and downstream throttles are separate; handle 429 responses with bounded backoff. Diagram: APIkey->usageplanmeter alongside separateJWT/IAMauthgate thenbackend; ratebucket andmonthlyquota targetnot hardcaplabels.

Budget for best effort: Usage-plan quotas and throttling are best effort, not hard spending caps. Regional/account and downstream throttles are separate; handle 429 responses with bounded backoff.
13.decisionCue: API keys support metering, not secure identity or a hard cost ceiling.

13.title: Diagnose API errors at the layer that produced them
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Inspect client-side failures: 400 can indicate invalid input; 401/403 can indicate authentication, policy, WAF or other access/path issues. A 429 may come from API throttles or downstream capacity. Inspect integration failures: A 502 often indicates a failed or malformed proxy response; 503 signals unavailability; a 504 can indicate integration timeout. Status alone is not a complete root cause. Correlate before retrying: Use request identifiers, access/execution logs, integration status and Lambda metrics. Retry only suitable failures with idempotency and investigate continuing work after timeouts. Diagram: Layereddiagnosticboard client/API/integration/Lambda with400403429502504 routedtolabeledchecks; noall502=orderclaim.

Inspect integration failures: A 502 often indicates a failed or malformed proxy response; 503 signals unavailability; a 504 can indicate integration timeout. Status alone is not a complete root cause.

Correlate before retrying: Use request identifiers, access/execution logs, integration status and Lambda metrics. Retry only suitable failures with idempotency and investigate continuing work after timeouts.
13.decisionCue: An HTTP code narrows the investigation; evidence identifies the cause.

13.title: API observability separates gateway time from backend time
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Log the right context: Supported access logs record request identifiers, caller context and status. REST execution logging can add integration detail; redact credentials and sensitive payloads. Compare latency layers: Gateway Latency and IntegrationLatency measure different portions of the path. Add 4XX/5XX counts, throttle signals and REST cache-hit/miss evidence. Respect product differences: REST supports execution logs, supported Firehose access-log delivery and X-Ray tracing. HTTP APIs have a leaner monitoring feature set; use current instrumentation guidance. Diagram: Six chronological events: API receives request, preprocessing, sends integration request, receives integration response, response processing, sends client response. Latency spans full gateway interval. IntegrationLatency spans only integration send to integration response. Separate logs/metrics/traces cards.

Compare latency layers: Gateway Latency and IntegrationLatency measure different portions of the path. Add 4XX/5XX counts, throttle signals and REST cache-hit/miss evidence.

Respect product differences: REST supports execution logs, supported Firehose access-log delivery and X-Ray tracing. HTTP APIs have a leaner monitoring feature set; use current instrumentation guidance.
13.decisionCue: Measure the gateway and integration separately before tuning either.

13.title: WebSocket routing handles a connection lifecycle
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Connect and authorize: Clients establish a wss connection. Authenticate at the supported connection gate and retain trusted user/tenant association with the connection identifier. Route messages: Use $connect, $disconnect and $default plus application routes selected from message content. Route handlers can use supported Lambda, HTTP or AWS integrations. Handle connection limits: Clients need reconnect and resubscribe behavior. Connection state in DynamoDB is an application record; disconnect delivery and cleanup still need robust handling. Diagram: Client<->WebSocket API with connect/message/disconnect routes to handlers and trusted connectionId state. Optional configured route response/callback. Reconnect originates client->API. No automatic frame implied from handler return.

Route messages: Use $connect, $disconnect and $default plus application routes selected from message content. Route handlers can use supported Lambda, HTTP or AWS integrations.
Handle connection limits: Clients need reconnect and resubscribe behavior. Connection state in DynamoDB is an application record; disconnect delivery and cleanup still need robust handling.
13.decisionCue: A persistent connection still needs lifecycle, authorization and recovery logic.

13.title: WebSocket callbacks use a signed HTTPS management request
13.imageBrief: Module09 style. Use the right endpoint: Clients use wss to connect. Backend callbacks use the HTTPS @connections management endpoint for the correct API, stage/custom-domain mapping and connection identifier. Authorize the backend: Sign management requests with SigV4 and scope execute-api:ManageConnections permissions. The original client token is not an automatic backend IAM permission. Handle stale connections: A callback can fail with GoneException if the client is gone or not yet established. Remove stale state and implement reconnect/recovery without blind repeated sends. Diagram: Client<->wssAPI persistentconnection; Lambda->signedHTTPSPOST /@connections/id ->API->client; DynamoDBidlookup; staleid -> Gone -> cleanup. NeverwsscallbackURL.
